activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: In a time signature, the top number gives the number of beats in each bar and the bottom number gives the note value that gets one beat, so 4/4 means four quarter-note beats.
story:
Nicolas sat at his grandmother's piano with a pencil behind his ear and a sheet of staff paper on the music stand, counting under his breath. The assignment from Ms. Vogel was due in nine days: sixteen bars, a melody with chord changes, written in standard notation, no recordings accepted. He had the piano, which was lucky, because his house had nothing but a battered guitar with five strings. His grandmother had offered the sunroom, where the light came through in long pale bars across the keys.

He had written four bars on Tuesday and crossed out three of them. The fourth bar he liked, a small rise and fall around a C chord, but when he played the line straight through it sounded like someone clearing their throat before never speaking. He wrote two more bars anyway, because Ms. Vogel had said the first draft should be bad, that the point of notation was to see what you'd actually done rather than what you remembered doing.

Emery arrived on Saturday with a backpack and a bag of clementines, having texted "I want to see this disaster." Nicolas played the six bars for him. Emery ate a clementine, spit a seed into his palm, and stared at the page upside down, which was how he claimed to read anything honestly.

"Okay, so what time signature is this in?" Emery asked, tapping the empty space at the start of the staff where the numbers should go.

"Four-four, obviously."

"Then why do half your bars have five beats in them?"

Nicolas pulled the paper close and counted bar three: quarter, quarter, half, and then a dotted half he'd written when the melody needed one more note than the bar could hold. He counted bar six. Five beats. He counted every bar and found three with too much in them, crammed like a closet.

"I put in whatever the melody wanted," he said.

"The bar doesn't want anything. That's the whole deal." Emery leaned over and drew a big 4 over a big 4 in the margin, uninvited. "The top number is how many beats are in each bar. The bottom number is which note gets one beat. So 4/4 means four quarter-note beats. Four of them. Per bar. You have five. You have a five-four situation pretending to be a four-four situation."

Nicolas looked at the numbers. He had known this, in the way he knew the boiling point of water, a fact stored somewhere it couldn't be reached while cooking. He tried counting the bars again with the rule in mind, tapping the pencil on the piano lid, and the extra beats stood out like a thread hanging off a hem.

His grandmother came through with laundry and stopped at the doorway, listening. She had played, decades ago, in a hotel bar with a trio, and Nicolas had once found a photo of her at twenty-three in a satin dress, mesemerized-looking, eyes half closed at the keys, though she'd said she'd mainly been tired. Now she said only, "The clock is a tyrant," and carried the basket upstairs.

Nicolas tried two fixes. First he cut notes until every bar had exactly four quarter-note beats, and played it, and it was correct and dead, the melody stopping and starting like a learner driver. Then he rewrote the whole thing in five, so that the top number matched what his hands wanted, and played that, and it moved, but it moved strangely, lopsided, a walk with one long leg. He sat with both versions on the stand side by side.

Emery, who had been scrolling through his phone for ten minutes, looked up. "Which one?"

"I don't know. The four is what people's feet expect. The five is what I actually hear." He played the last phrase of each version. "Maybe the answer is that the melody is wrong. Not the bar. I was so sure the idea was the part that mattered and the notation was just the paperwork."

"Ms. Vogel's going to say something about the idea being nothing until it's shareable."

"I know. And I think she's right, and I also think she's wrong." Nicolas took the pencil from behind his ear. He had started the week thinking music was a feeling you transcribed, and now it seemed more like a substrate, something the feeling had to sit on top of, level and measured, or it spilled. But when he looked at his lopsided five-four version he could hear a shape that the grid hadn't put there either. Both things were true and he could not make them be the same thing.

Emery peeled another clementine. "You could also just write sixteen terrible bars and call it jazz."

"That's not what jazz is."

"I know. I'm being hedonistic about your homework. It's Saturday."

Nicolas laughed, then pulled the five-four sheet off the stand and laid it flat on the sunroom table, and above the first staff he wrote a small, definite 5 over 4. He tapped four quarter notes into his left hand against his knee, then a fifth, then again, and began playing the melody slowly to that new pulse, watching his grandmother's laundry line turn slowly in the wind outside the window, one sheet, then another, then a gap.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Negative space is the empty area around and between the subjects of an image, and artists often draw that space to get a shape's outline right.
story:
Eli had promised Mr. Nakamura a pen-and-ink drawing of the old kitchen chair from the neighbor's porch, a going-away present for a man who was moving to his daughter's city in eleven days, and the chair kept defeating him. Four attempts lay scattered across the kitchen table, each one wrong in a way he couldn't name. The legs splayed like a drunk spider. The seat tilted though he had measured it twice with a ruler. His mother drifted through for coffee and said, kindly, that the fourth one was better, but Eli could see she was being effusive the way she was with young children's finger paintings, and it stung more than criticism would have.

He texted Peyton, whose sketches filled the margins of every worksheet they shared in physics. "How do you draw a chair without it looking haunted." The reply came in bubbles, then a paragraph, then a photo of her own failed chair, which made him feel briefly less alone. Then a second message arrived, longer, and he read it twice at the table with the phone propped against the salt shaker.

"Okay so my aunt taught me this and it sounds fake but it isn't. Negative space is the empty area around and between the subjects of an image. Artists draw that space to get a shape's outline right. So instead of the chair, draw the gaps. The triangles between the legs. The hole under the seat where you can see the wall. Trust me. Try it before you decide I'm insane."

He sat with that for a moment. It felt like a trick, and also like the kind of heuristic that might actually hold weight, a shortcut that could be tested rather than believed. The interesting part was that it asked him to stop looking at the thing itself. What if the shape of the chair lived in everything the chair wasn't?

He fetched the chair from the porch, set it against the plain wall by the window, and pinned fresh paper to his board. He started with the gap between the front legs, a tall triangle with a slice cut out of it where the crossbar interrupted. He drew only the gaps after that: the rectangles of wall showing through the back spindles, the awkward hexagon of floor visible beneath the seat. It was strangely calming, like doing a puzzle whose picture didn't matter. When he stepped back, the chair was there, unmistakably there, standing solid in the middle of a drawing of nothing.

Peyton called while he was inking the wall spaces solid black, and he put her on speaker. "It worked," he said. "I don't fully get why." "You don't have to get why," she said. "You just have to keep drawing the empty parts until the real part shows up." He told her about the gift for Mr. Nakamura, and she asked whether he was drawing the man's chair or his own, and Eli said the man's, obviously, and there was a pause on the line long enough that he heard her breathing. "Just asking," she said. "Because your chair is different. The gap under your seat is bigger." She was teasing, mostly, but after he hung up he found himself comparing the two chairs in his head, the porch one and the one at their kitchen table, and noticing that the space between a chair's legs was a little like a signature, no two exactly the same.

He thought, while the ink dried, about his father, who had been gone since spring and who Eli had not forgiven, and whom Eli suspected he would have to forgive anyway, not because it was deserved but because carrying it to college in the fall seemed like packing a stone in an already full bag. Maybe that was another way of drawing the gaps. You couldn't fix the thing directly, so you worked at everything around it and hoped the outline would emerge. He wasn't sure that was true. It might be a lazy borrowing from a drawing trick that only worked on chairs. But he wrote his father a short email that night, the first in four months, saying the car had passed inspection and asking, in the last line, whether he still had the blue chair from the garage. Then he sat with his cursor over the send button for a long moment before the click.

In the morning the drawing was finished, chair-shaped by way of all its emptiness, and he carried it across the yard in a cardboard folder. Mr. Nakamura was wrapping dishes in newspaper at his kitchen counter, and when he opened the folder he was quiet in a way that made Eli nervous, until the old man said, "You drew my chair better than a photograph would," and began clearing a space on the counter to look at it properly. "There's something else in it," Mr. Nakamura said, tilting his head. "Something around the chair." He tapped the black shapes between the legs with one finger. "What do you call this part?" Eli looked at the empty spaces, which were somehow the fullest ones, and opened his mouth.

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: In the United States, the Department of Housing and Urban Development considers a household cost-burdened if it spends more than 30 percent of its income on housing.
story:
The bank smelled like carpet cleaner and cold air, and Gabriella had the two leases laid out on the counter by the deposit slips because the table by the window was taken. Kabir stood beside her with a calculator app open, thumb hovering.

"Okay," she said. "The one on Mercer Street is eleven hundred a month but utilities are included. The one near campus is nine fifty, plus electric, plus water, plus internet."

"So we add them up."

"So we add them up, but we have to guess the utilities, because neither of them will tell me until I live there." She had emailed both property managers and gotten one auto-reply and one paragraph of cheerful nothing. "The Mercer one, we don't have to guess. That's the whole point of it."

Kabir typed while she read numbers off. "So worst case, if electric runs like a hundred twenty in summer, water maybe forty, internet sixty."

"Say sixty for internet because that's the plan I'd get anyway." She watched him add it. "Eleven seventy."

"Which is more than eleven hundred."

"By seventy dollars." She said it flatly, the way you say something so it doesn't sound like a victory, because it wasn't one yet. Seventy dollars a month was eight hundred forty a year, and she had eight hundred forty dollars in the savings account she'd opened at this same branch the summer she turned fifteen.

The memory arrived the way they do, without permission. She was sixteen, at the teller window with a paycheque from the ice cream shop, and Ms. Ndlovu had been behind her in line. Ms. Ndlovu taught government at the high school and lived two doors down, and she had looked at the cheque, then at Gabriella, and said only, "Save some before it turns into shoes." Gabriella had laughed and then, walking home, had transferred forty percent into savings, mostly to have a story about being responsible. It had felt like a costume then. She wondered, now, at the little counter by the deposit slips, whether it still was.

"The other thing," Kabir said, "is your paycheque. You make what, fourteen an hour, twenty hours?"

"Fifteen now. Twenty, sometimes twenty-five." She did the math on the back of the Mercer lease, where there was blank margin. Four weeks at twenty hours, six hundred a week, twenty-four hundred a month, before taxes took their quiet share. She wrote the real number lower, maybe two thousand. Then she divided eleven seventy into two thousand and got close to fifty-nine percent, and nine fifty plus no utilities, just to see, was still forty-seven and a half.

"That's a lot," Kabir said, reading over her arm.

"There's a thing for this," she said slowly. "I read it when I was looking stuff up. The Department of Housing and Urban Development, they consider a household cost-burdened if it spends more than thirty percent of its income on housing."

"Cost-burdened." He said the word like he was testing its weight. "That's either of them, then. Both of them."

"Both of them. Even the cheap one, even before utilities." She looked at the numbers and let them sit there instead of trying to metabolize them into something softer, because she was tired of doing that, tired of rounding her own life down until it looked affordable. Her mother did it constantly, called every rent "doable" in a voice with a diminuendo at the end of the word, the confidence trailing off exactly where the arithmetic started.

"Could you get more hours," Kabir said. It wasn't really a question; it was him being kind in the shape of a question.

"Then I'm working thirty hours and taking five classes." She thought of the virulent little voice in her head that said other people manage it, the one that sounded suspiciously like her aunt, and she refused to hand it the microphone. "Or I get a roommate for Mercer. It's a two-bedroom. Split eleven hundred, that's five fifty each, utilities included, that's twenty-seven and a half percent."

"Under the line."

"Under the line. By two and a half points." She wrote it in the margin and then, because she was being honest with herself for once, wrote the thing she didn't want to write: roommate unknown. Whoever it was could be loud, could be late with their half, could leave dishes in the sink until the sink itself gave up. The seventy dollars had been a solved problem. This one had a person-shaped hole in it.

She folded both leases and put them in her backpack, the creases already soft from a week of handling. The teller called number forty-two, and an old man went up with his Social Security cheque held out like a ticket.

"I'll ask Shayan," she said. "He needs a place too, and he does dishes. I've seen him do dishes."

Kabir put his phone away. "Then Mercer wins?"

"I don't know yet. Ask me Thursday." She zipped the backpack and picked it up, and the automatic doors opened onto the parking lot, hot and bright, her bus already pulling in.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: A research paper's thesis must be arguable, a claim a reasonable person could dispute, rather than a fact everyone already accepts.
story:
The draft came back on a Thursday, folded once, with Mr. Gupta's green pen circling the first sentence and a single word in the margin: "So?" Madeline read it in the hallway outside the gym, twice, then a third time, because it seemed impossible that eleven pages could be dismissed in two letters. Her thesis, underlined twice for confidence, stated that the Northwest Rebellion of 1885 involved Métis grievances over land and the railway. She knew this was true. She had footnoted it nine times.

She had planned to spend the weekend at her own house, but her mother was painting the kitchen and had decreed, with the finality of a person holding a roller, that Madeline would be happier at her grandmother's. So Friday afternoon she rode two buses out past the hardware store that used to be a bank, carrying her laptop, both library books, and the folded draft, which she had begun to think of as a small injured animal.

Her grandmother's house smelled of celery seed and newsprint. Madeline set up at the dining room table under the light fixture with the amber shades, and her grandmother brought tea Madeline didn't ask for and then left her alone, which was the correct amount of attention. Maxime texted a photo of himself at Fraser's, both of them gesturing at a half-built bookshelf, captioned "the paper going well then?" She put the phone face down.

The problem, once she opened the document and stared at the circled sentence, was that she couldn't find the argument because she had never believed there was one to find. Land and railway, grievances, 1885: these were facts, sitting in her paper like stones in a garden. She had arranged them carefully. She had cited them in the style the handout prescribed, commas in the right kingdoms. Somewhere, she suspected, in some incipient form, an actual claim existed, but every time she reached for it, it moved a little further into the dark.

On Saturday her grandmother's neighbour, Mr. Gupta, came by to return a casserole dish, and Madeline, who had been informed at the door that he taught at the college, waylaid him in the hall with her laptop like a process server. He read the circled sentence while holding the dish at hip level. "This isn't a thesis," he said. "It's a fact. Nobody reasonable would dispute it." He looked at her over the screen. "A thesis has to be arguable. Something a sensible person could actually disagree with." Then he asked about her grandmother's hydrangeas and left with the dish still in his hands, having said nothing further, which Madeline later understood was a kind of gift.

She sat with that. Arguable. It sounded quarrelsome to her, and she didn't like quarrelling; she liked being right in a quiet way that allayed the need for anyone to say so. But arguable wasn't the same as combative, she decided somewhere between lunch and the second cup of tea. It meant the paper had to be worth disagreeing with. She wrote, crossed out, wrote again. The railroad caused the rebellion. Too big, probably, and the footnotes wouldn't carry it. The Métis response was justified. That was arguable, and also enormous, and also, she noticed, a question of values rather than evidence, and her evidence was eleven footnotes about land scrip.

By evening she had it narrowed to something she could defend and still sleep: that the government's timing, the sequence of decisions, mattered more than the grievances themselves, which both sides already knew about. The grievances were the stones; her claim was about who set them, and in what order, and to what end. She couldn't prove it completely. She could show the pattern and admit the gap, which felt, unexpectedly, more honest than the eleven pages of arranged certainty had. Maxime texted again, a photo of the finished bookshelf leaning visibly to the left, and Fraser in the background saying something about load-bearing.

Her grandmother came through with the watering can around nine and read the new first paragraph standing up, tilting her head at it.

"What's it arguing?" her grandmother asked.

"That the order of events mattered," Madeline said. "Not just the events."

Her grandmother considered this while watering a plant that clearly didn't need it. "Your grandfather argued about everything," she said finally. "I used to think it was rude. Turns out he was just thesis material." She set down the can and tapped the page with one finger, near the margin, where the green "So?" was still visible through Madeline's new draft, and left her to it, tea going cold, cursor blinking in the amber light.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: A blood pressure reading gives two numbers in millimeters of mercury: systolic pressure when the heart beats, over diastolic pressure when the heart relaxes between beats.
story:
I knew the material cold, or that was the story I told myself all week while the rest of the class panicked about the practical. The unit test on blood pressure counted for a quarter of our grade, and Mr. Korhonen had a way of looking at you when you got something wrong, that patient, disappointed half-smile, which was worse than shouting. So I told Kiara I was fine, twice, until she stopped asking.

The truth was I had the two numbers backward in my head and I knew it, the way you know a tooth is cracked. Somewhere in my notes, top and bottom had swapped positions, and every time I tried to fix it, my memory insisted on its own version. On Saturday my grandmother came over, and while my mother was out getting groceries, Grandma sat at the kitchen table with the little wrist cuff my uncle had mailed her from the pharmacy, pushing the button like it might bite.

"Brooke, what does this mean," she said. "One hundred forty-two over ninety."

I could have said I didn't know. Instead I pulled out a chair beside her, because there was something in me that wanted to be the person who knew, even when I wasn't.

The machine's screen glowed on the table between us. I turned my notebook to the page where I'd copied the diagram from the board, two numbers stacked like a fraction, and I made myself slow down and read it properly instead of reciting from the broken file in my head. The reading gives two numbers in millimeters of mercury. The top one, the systolic, is the pressure when the heart beats. The bottom one, the diastolic, is when the heart relaxes between beats. I said it to myself twice. It was the opposite of what I'd been telling myself all week, and the floor of my confidence gave way all at once, a visceral drop, like missing a stair in the dark.

"It's systolic over diastolic," I said out loud, because saying it was the only way to make it stick. "The top number is when your heart beats. The bottom one is when it rests between beats."

"So which one is mine?" Grandma tapped the screen with one finger.

"Both are yours. The top is the beating one, one hundred forty-two. The bottom is the resting one, ninety." I watched her face to see whether it had landed. She nodded slowly, the way she nodded at weather.

"And is that good, that the resting one is ninety?"

There it was, the question I couldn't answer, because Mr. Korhonen had only given us the structure of the reading, not the judgments, and I wasn't going to guess at my grandmother's health from a worksheet. I had a memory of him starting to expatiate on diet and exercise during Thursday's class, something about how regular movement and what you eat can change the numbers over time, and then the fire alarm went off, and we never got the rest. That was the part I kept circling. I trusted the structure, the two numbers, the beating and the resting, because I had just reassembled it in front of her. The rest was logos without its conclusion, an argument missing its final line.

"I don't know yet," I said. "That's honest. But I know how to read it now, and when I find out what the numbers should be, I'll tell you."

She laughed, a short dry sound. "Your mother says the same thing about her recipes."

Here is where I have to admit what kind of narrator I am. All week I'd been telling people I was prepared, and the moment that mattered, the moment my grandmother actually needed something, I'd nearly given her the two numbers reversed, heart beating for resting, resting for beating, and she would have gone home believing it. The problem wasn't the test. The problem was that I'd rather look prepared than be it, and that had almost become a fact about somebody's heart.

So I called Kiara from the kitchen, standing by the window over the sink. "I had it backward," I said. "The top number is systolic, when the heart beats. The bottom is diastolic, when it relaxes between beats. Say it back to me."

"You had it backward this whole time?" Kiara's voice had that rising note of delight I both loved and resented.

"Say it back."

"Top is the beat, bottom is the rest. There. You owe me a coffee." She paused. "You told me you were fine."

"I told me I was fine. That's the problem."

I hung up and wrote the corrected version across the whole top of the page in capital letters, then copied it onto a fresh card for Grandma to keep in her purse beside her reading glasses. She watched me write, hands folded on the table, the cuff lying dark and quiet between us.

"For the test," she asked, "or for me?"

I slid the card across the table to her.

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: A security deposit is held to cover unpaid rent or damage beyond normal wear and tear, so in many jurisdictions a landlord cannot deduct for ordinary aging like small nail holes.
story:
The real estate office sat between a nail salon and a defunct yogurt shop, and Nicholas had spent every Tuesday and Thursday since September behind its front desk, sorting listings for Ms. Clarke-Williams and learning, without anyone intending to teach him, the vocabulary of shelter. He learned that rent was what you paid to occupy something that belonged to someone else, and that a mortgage was what you paid when the bank let you pretend the place was yours. He learned that first-time buyers arrived believing a down payment was a fee, like a ticket, rather than a fraction of the price you handed over up front so the bank would trust you with the rest. He filed the papers of a couple who had saved eleven years for theirs, and he filed the papers of a man who walked in with a cashier's check and a face like someone surrendering.

In October his mother told him, over canned soup, that the building on Corrigan Street had been sold and everyone had ninety days. She had signed the lease at twenty-two, back when the apartment had been a way station, and then the way station had reified itself, quietly, into a life: his height marked in pencil on the kitchen doorframe, her books double-stacked in the hall. "They'll want the deposit back," she said. "Whatever's left of it."

Nicholas knew the word deposit the way he knew the word mortgage, which was to say not at all until it applied to him. He asked Isabela, who worked the afternoon shift and was saving for an apartment of her own with the grim discipline of someone training for a war. "It's money the landlord holds," she said, counting brochures. "A security deposit. It covers unpaid rent or damage beyond normal wear and tear." She slapped a rubber band around the stack. "But not ordinary aging. Small nail holes count as ordinary. Everyone gets that wrong."

He looked at her. "So they can't just take it for nail holes?"

"That's what I said." She glanced up. "Why."

He didn't answer, because the answer was that his mother had spent two weeks filling nail holes with toothpaste, badly, and had gone quiet when he asked whether that was how it was done. On Saturday he rode the bus to Corrigan Street with his phone and photographed every wall in the apartment, every scuffed baseboard, the doorframe with his pencil marks, the window latch that had been broken since he was nine. He shot wide and then close, and he made his mother stand in the doorway of the kitchen for scale, and she laughed at him once, quietly, and then let him finish.

The landlord's letter arrived the following week. Deductions for wall repair, it said, for the nail holes, for repainting a unit that had not been repainted in fourteen years. His mother read it at the table and set it down and said it was probably fair, probably how it worked, and Nicholas felt something hot climb his neck, because he knew, now, that the letter was a travesty of how it worked, dressed in the language of how it worked. He printed his photographs at the library, twenty-two of them, and stapled them to a letter he drafted three times. When his mother asked what he was doing he said, "Demand letter," and she said, "Since when do you write demand letters," and he said, "Since Tuesdays and Thursdays."

At the office, Alexzander, who was studying for a real estate license the way other seniors studied for the SAT, looked over the draft and pronounced it "a little tautological, honestly, you keep saying the deposit is the deposit," but he didn't say it was wrong. Ms. Clarke-Williams came out of her office with a coffee, read a single paragraph over Nicholas's shoulder, and said nothing except "Send it certified," and went back in. The landlord's reply came nine days later: a check for the full deposit, minus nothing, and a sentence about wishing the tenant well that read as though it had been written by a lawyer holding his nose.

His mother used part of it on the new place's first month and put the rest in an envelope marked house, which Nicholas understood to be aspirational rather than arithmetic. Eleven years, he thought, like the couple with the closing papers. He was still thinking about it on a Thursday in December when a woman came in with her daughter, maybe ten years old, and asked Ms. Clarke-Williams how much a person needed to buy something small, just small, and Ms. Clarke-Williams said that depended, and pulled out a chair, and Nicholas watched from the desk as the woman sat down and opened a notebook already full of numbers.

He took out his phone and, under a listing for a two-bedroom no one had rented yet, started a note of his own.

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: Of the common disturbances to an equilibrium, a change in temperature is the only one that changes the value of the equilibrium constant K.
story:
Brianna's display table sat three rows from the gymnasium doors, where every draft from the hallway found her poster board and lifted its corners. Her project was modest beside the others, an ascetic arrangement of beakers, a hot plate, and one hand-lettered chart, but it was hers down to the last data point: cobalt chloride solution shifting between pink and blue as she pushed the equilibrium one way and pulled it back. The judge was due in twenty minutes, and Umar had just handed her a folded note.

"Read it before Silva gets here," he said, and drifted back toward his own table, where his volcano sat inert and unjudged.

The note was written in his cramped pencil. He had entered the regional qualifier early, before the school fair, and had failed the equilibrium section completely. He'd cooled a reaction and then, on the next question, heated it and used the same K, the same equilibrium constant, because that was the number the textbook had given him. Every answer after that came out wrong. He'd been too embarrassed to tell her until now, and he wanted her to check her chart before Mr. Silva, who was judging the chemistry row this year, noticed what he had noticed too late.

Brianna read it twice. Her chart listed her calculated K values beside each temperature trial, and she had done what he had done, carried the constant across like luggage that never changed weight. She flipped back through her lab notebook. At room temperature, the equilibrium sat where the books said it should. When she warmed the solution, the color change told her the equilibrium had shifted, but she had recorded the same K for the warm trials, assuming the shift balanced out, that nothing underneath the color had really changed.

She looked down the row. Laetitia was at her own table, calibrating a pH probe with maddening patience, and Brianna called her over anyway.

"When you heat your reaction," Brianna asked, keeping her voice low, "does your K stay the same?"

"Yours doesn't?" Laetitia glanced at the chart, then at the notebook, then at her. "Mine does. But I only change concentrations, and adding more stuff doesn't touch K. Heating's different. Temperature is the only thing that actually changes it."

Brianna stood very still while the gym noise went on around her, the bleachers creaking, someone's buzzer going off at the physics tables. Concentration, pressure, those pushed the equilibrium one way or the other and it settled again, same constant underneath. Temperature remade the constant itself. Which meant every shifted prediction she had charted for the heated trials was built on a number that no longer applied. She thought of Umar's note, of him sitting in that exam hall multiplying by a K that heat had already dissolved, and the coincidence felt less like luck than something harder, a synchronicity that had put both of them at the same table, three weeks apart, with the same wrong assumption. It did not portend anything good for the judging.

Mr. Silva was two tables away. She had minutes, not hours. Brianna pulled the marker from her apron pocket and turned the chart over to its blank back, drawing the axis freehand, plotting the values she could salvage from the color-intensity photos she'd taken at each temperature. The trend wasn't precise, and she knew it. She could show that K changed with temperature, but not exactly how much, not without redoing trials she had no time to redo. When Mr. Silva arrived, tugging his lanyard straight, she had the new chart taped crooked over the old one and her notebook open to the flawed pages, deliberately, so he could see both.

"Walk me through it," he said.

She told him about the note, and Umar's exam, and her own chart, and what she had crossed out. She pointed to the blank spaces on the new plot where the data should be. "I know temperature shifts the equilibrium," she said. "What I know better now is that it changes K itself, and I don't know the new values yet. Those gaps are honest."

Mr. Silva looked at the crooked tape, the crossed-out column, the blank spaces. Down the row, Umar had turned from his volcano to watch, and Laetitia's probe finally blinked steady green.

"Show me the hot plate," Mr. Silva said. "Heat it up. Let's see what it does."

Brianna plugged it in.

activity: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
knowledge_domain: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
fact: In 1936 the Literary Digest poll collected about 2.4 million responses yet predicted that Alf Landon would beat Franklin Roosevelt, who then won in a landslide.
story:
The folding chairs at Jefferson Middle School smelled of floor wax and old rain, and Noah had been standing behind the bake-sale table since seven, holding a clipboard he did not entirely believe in. Mr. Abdi had assigned them an exit poll for statistics class: stand outside the gym where the city voted, ask every fifth person how they had cast their ballot on the school levy, and tabulate. Noah's mother had come through at eight-fifteen and refused to tell him anything, which he suspected was her idea of a joke. "You'll find out when everyone else does," she said, patting his head like he was six.

The trouble had started the night before, in the group chat, when Shiloh posted a link to an online survey with a number in the corner so large it looked like a typo. Two point four million responses, and it said the levy was going down by eleven points. "You can't argue with that," Shiloh had typed. "Our thing is what, forty people? That's a rounding error on a rounding error." Zainab had replied with a single eye-roll emoji, which was not, strictly speaking, an argument.

By mid-morning they had forty-three responses, and the tally sheet was too close to mean anything. Zainab leaned over Noah's shoulder, chewing the end of a pen she had borrowed from the sign-in table. "Thirty-one yes, twelve no, give or take."

"Give or take what," Noah said. "That's the whole question."

She flipped the clipboard around and tapped the sheet, where she had written the words margin of error with a question mark after them, copied off a polling report someone had left on the bake-sale table. The report described a survey of eight hundred likely voters, and after its numbers it said the margin of error was about three points, and that the true value could fall on either side. Noah read it twice. Forty-three people, he thought, could not even pretend to have a margin that small. The phrase had a humility to it that Shiloh's two point four million, shouting from the phone in all caps, did not.

Zainab, meanwhile, had not stopped thinking about Shiloh, or about the group chat, which had gone quiet after his last message. She knew him well enough to know that quiet meant confident. She also knew that confidence was not the same as being right, though she could not have said where the difference lived. "Ask your grandfather's book thing," she said to Noah. "The one you were telling me about."

Noah had found it in June, in a box of his grandfather's paperbacks, while packing the apartment after the move. He had read it in two nights mostly because the room had no internet yet. It was about the 1936 election, and one chapter had a poll by a magazine called the Literary Digest, which had collected about 2.4 million responses and predicted that Alf Landon would beat Franklin Roosevelt. Roosevelt then won in a landslide. Noah had sat on the floor of the empty room and read the sentence four times. Two point four million people, and the poll still got the direction of the whole thing backwards.

He told it now, out loud, standing under the hand-lettered VOTE HERE sign, feeling the story arrive in the right order for once. Shiloh, who had shown up at noon with a box of donuts and the confidence of a man bearing gifts, stopped mid-donut.

"So millions of people can be wrong," Shiloh said slowly. "Not wrong. The people answered. The poll was wrong."

"And I can't tell you why," Noah said. "The book didn't hold my hand, and I'm not going to hold yours. But it's the same number as your survey, and your survey says eleven points, and honestly, man, I don't think we know anything."

Mr. Abdi came out of the gym with a paper cup of bad coffee and stood in the doorway, listening, saying nothing, which was his way of grading. The line inside had shortened. A woman Noah recognized from the bus, the one who always carried a folded bicycle helmet, pushed through the doors and stopped at their table.

"Every fifth person," Noah said. "It's for a class. How did you vote on the levy?"

She looked at his clipboard, then at Zainab's margin-of-error question mark, then at Shiloh's donuts.

"Wrong woman," she said. "I'm number six."

Zainab wrote down her answer anyway.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Gluten forms when the wheat proteins glutenin and gliadin mix with water, and kneading longer makes the gluten network stronger and the bread chewier.
story:
The pasta machine had not been used since the summer before Ryder's grandfather died. It sat on the top shelf of the pantry at his grandmother's house, chrome gone dull, its crank handle wrapped in a rubber band that had dried and cracked. Ryder took it down on a Tuesday in July because his mother had said, on the phone, that somebody should cook for Grandma, and because he had promised himself he would learn to make bread before he left for college.

The first loaf came out of the oven flat and tight, a brick with a crust. When he cut into it, the crumble fell apart on the board like wet sand. His grandmother ate a piece anyway, buttered, and said it was fine, which he understood to mean it was not. He had followed the recipe. He had measured the flour twice. What he had not done was knead it long, because his arms had gotten tired around minute four and the dough had looked smooth enough, and he had wanted to believe that looking smooth was the same as being done.

He sat on the back steps with his phone and read until the screen dimmed. Flour, water, salt, yeast: that was the whole list, so the difference had to be in the doing. He learned that gluten forms when the wheat proteins glutenin and gliadin mix with water, and that kneading longer makes the gluten network stronger and the bread chewier. He read the sentence three times, then closed the phone and looked at the yard, where his grandfather's tomato stakes still stood in their crooked rows.

"You're making another one," his grandmother said from the doorway. It was not a question.

"I got the first one wrong."

"The first one was fine."

"It was dense because I stopped too early. There's these proteins, glutenin and gliadin, they're in the flour already. They just need water and time." He heard his own voice go flat, like he was reading aloud, and he stopped. "I'm going to knead this one for ten full minutes."

She came and sat beside him, which she did not usually do in the afternoon; her hip bothered her after lunch. "Your grandfather used to say you can't hurry dough or grief. I thought it was just something old men said." She picked at the rubber band on the crank handle until it snapped off. "Maybe there's a reason they say it."

On Thursday, Elia came over with a bag of apricots from her aunt's tree, and Maddie came because Elia came. Maddie wanted to make noodles, which was why the pasta machine was on the counter. They took turns feeding dough through the rollers while Ryder worked his bread on the board, folding it over, pushing with the heel of his hand, turning it a quarter turn, folding again. The dough fought him at first, tearing when he stretched it, snapping back. Then, somewhere past the middle, it stopped fighting. It stretched thin enough to let the window light through without breaking.

"Look at that," Elia said. She held a sheet of pasta up to the window so it glowed, then fed it into the cutting attachment and turned the crank. The machine extruded long fettuccine ribbons onto the floured tray, one after another, in an even rhythm. "Your grandfather kept this thing greased."

"It's the same thing," Ryder said. "The noodles and the bread. It's the same proteins. You just work them longer for the noodles."

Maddie, who had been quiet, said she had always thought chewy was a bad thing in bread. Ryder started to answer and then did not, because he had been thinking the same thing all morning. The first loaf had been crumbly, and crumbly was wrong, but chewy was what his grandfather's bread had been, the loaves he remembered from before, and he had liked the crumbly one fine with butter. Strength in the network meant toughness in the crumb. He stood at the board with the dough under his hands, both things true at once, and no way to hold them except to keep kneading.

The second loaf rose higher than the first, and the crust cracked along the top where it had split in the oven, which the recipe called good. When it had cooled enough, he cut it, and the knife met resistance all the way down, and the slice bent without shattering. His grandmother took her piece to the table without comment. Maddie chewed hers slowly, and Elia tore hers and dragged it through the pasta water, and outside the screen door the tomatoes were coming in late and hard, determined anyway.

Grandma turned her slice over once, examining the holes in it, the even, open crumb. "Chewier," she said. "That's what you wanted?"

"That's what the kneading does." He buttered a second slice. "The other one was easier to eat, though. I haven't decided which one I'd make again."

She ate a bite, then another. "Make both," she said. "One for eating, one for remembering. Now sit down before it's gone."

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: Research by Gabriele Wulf found that learners usually improve faster when told to focus on the effect of a movement, such as the target, rather than on their own body parts.
story:
Hailey printed the drill plan at her kitchen table at eleven the night before, then folded it into her jacket pocket and forgot about it until she was standing at the boards of the community rink with nine ten-year-olds staring at her. The head coach, Ms. Wang, had given her the passing drills for the first half hour. "Their passing is the weakness," Ms. Wang had said. "Everything else can wait." Then she had gone to the far end to work with the goalies, and Hailey was on her own.

She started with the first drill, the one she had written out in careful numbered steps. Partners, ten feet apart, saucer pass over a glove laid on the ice. She skated along the line correcting them. "Bend your wrist more." "Turn your blade over at the end." "Keep your elbows in." She said these things because they were what her own coaches had said to her for years, and saying them felt like coaching. The kids nodded and kept making the same flat passes, pucks skittering wide of the glove, wobbling onto their edges.

Georgia was her first test case. Georgia was ten and could not receive a pass without dropping her stick an inch at the last second, so that the puck slid under it and away. Hailey crouched beside her and said, "Watch your blade angle when it comes in." Georgia looked at her blade. She looked at it so hard that she missed the next pass entirely, and the one after that ricocheted off her skate.

Karma was on the bench lacing her skates, and she was the one who said it. Karma was twelve, an assistant helper who had been assigned to Hailey the way schools assign anything, by a clipboard. "My skating coach last year told my mom something," Karma said, pulling her laces tight with her whole body. "There's research by somebody called Gabriele Wulf. Learners improve faster when they focus on the effect of the movement instead of their own body parts. Like the target. Not your wrists. The target."

Hailey said, "That's it?" "That's it," Karma said. "Mom taped it to the fridge."

So Hailey stood in front of the line and changed the words. "New rule," she said. "Nobody talks about wrists or elbows or blades. When you pass, you hit your teammate's hands. That's all you think about. The puck goes to her hands." She pointed at a girl with yellow tape on her shaft. "You're the target. Stand still." Then she sent them through the same drill, ten feet apart, glove on the ice, and watched.

The change was not instant. Two kids still stared down at their own sticks out of habit, and one boy asked, "But how do I bend my wrist without thinking about it?" and Hailey said, "You don't. Just hit her hands," which she delivered with more certainty than she felt. But by the third round, the passes were arriving. Not all of them, and not cleanly, but arriving. Georgia caught four in a row. On the fifth, she was so busy watching the incoming puck that she forgot to drop her stick, and it came to her tape and stayed.

Hailey skated a slow loop around the zone while they worked, saying the new words over and over. Hit the hands. Pass to the target, not to your own body. She was honest with herself about what she didn't know: maybe the kids were just getting tired of the old drill and a novelty effect was doing the work. Maybe Wulf's research was about golf or something and she was stretching it past what it covered. She had no way to tell, in one practice, which was which. She decided she was sanguine about that, mostly. Sanguine was a word from her vocabulary list, and using it correctly in her head was its own small satisfaction, but it also happened to be true. She could live with an experiment that hadn't finished.

The accounts could not be lived with so easily. At the break, Ms. Wang came over with the goalie coach's clipboard and said the association had sent a notice about registration fees, that four families hadn't paid, and that the word the treasurer kept using was insolvency, which Hailey had to look up later on her phone in the warming room: unable to pay debts. The team might fold by February. She filed this away and went back out.

She ran a final drill she invented on the spot, a three-on-one keepaway where the rule was that a pass counted only if it landed on the receiver's stick without her reaching for it. "Hands," she kept saying from the circle. "Aim at the hands." The kids picked up the chant themselves, shouting it at each other, enthralling themselves in their own noise the way ten-year-olds do, and the puck began to move around the triangle faster than it had all winter, faster than it had any right to move given who was passing it.

Ms. Wang stopped at the blue line and watched for a full minute without saying anything. Then she waved Hailey over. "Write down what you did differently," she said. "I want it for Thursday."

"I changed the words," Hailey said. "That's all I changed."

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: US employers withhold 6.2 percent of an employee's wages for Social Security tax, up to a yearly wage limit.
story:
The application had asked for his shirt size before it asked anything else, which should have warned him. Alex signed the forms at the popcorn counter on a Tuesday afternoon while the manager, a soft-spoken man named only in Alex's head as the manager, tapped a pen against the register. The job was concessions at the Regal-style theater two bus stops from school, minimum wage, weekends and two weeknights. He started Thursday. By the second Thursday he could fill a large bucket without looking, and by the third he had stopped flinching when the popper spat.

His first paycheck came as a slim envelope tucked into his cubby behind the ticket booth. He opened it in the lobby, near the standee for a movie he would never see, and stood very still. He had done the math on the bus that morning: fifty-one hours at his rate, minus nothing, because he had not thought there was a minus. The number on the check was smaller. Not catastrophically. Just smaller, in the way that a door left open a crack lets in cold.

He found Emiliano sweeping aisle four. Emiliano had been there eight months, wore a name tag with a smiley face drawn over the E, and claimed to have opinions about everything, most of them loud. "They shorted you," Emiliano said immediately, leaning on the broom. "Everyone thinks that the first time. Then everyone finds out, and then everyone forgets to tell the next person." He would not say more. He said the break room was where that kind of conversation happened, and the break room was, at that moment, occupied by two ushers Alex did not yet know well enough to interrupt.

The withholding haunted the rest of his shift. He poured, he made change, he apologized for the price of the candy, which was not his fault and which customers seemed determined to vilify him for personally, as though he had set the prices from his bedroom. Between rushes he ran the arithmetic on the back of a receipt. The difference was not a round number. It was a percentage of something, and it kept almost coming out to a familiar fraction before sliding away.

Rachelle found him after the nine o'clock showing let out. She had gotten him the interview in the first place, because her aunt had worked here and because Rachelle believed, with a confidence Alex both admired and distrusted, in the moral value of having a job at seventeen. He showed her the check and the hours and the receipt full of arithmetic. She frowned at it the way she frowned at bad grammar, personally offended. "That's less than what you earned," she said. "That's just true."

"I know it's less. I want to know where it went."

"Maybe it's a fee. Maybe they charge you for the shirt."

The shirt theory died in the break room the next night. One of the ushers, a college student everyone called by her last initial, was eating yogurt and reading something dense for a class, a casebook with jurisprudence in the title, and Alex, careful not to interrupt, waited until she looked up. He asked whether the theater charged for uniforms. She said no. He showed her the check. She glanced at his pay stub, at the small printed columns he had not thought to read closely, and slid it back across the table.

"Social Security," she said. "It's on there."

He looked. It was on there, in the smallest print on the stub, a line item and a number that matched his mystery almost exactly. He took out his phone and did the rest himself, dividing the difference by his gross pay, and the figure that surfaced was 6.2 percent. Six point two. He checked it twice. Emiliano leaned over his shoulder and nodded slowly, the way people nod when they are learning the thing they had promised to explain.

"The weird part," Emiliano said, "is my cousin makes real money, like at a warehouse, and hers stops. Later in the year it just stops coming out."

"Stops how?"

"There's a limit. Some yearly limit on your wages, and after that they don't take it anymore. She said the checks get bigger near the end of the year and it freaked her out."

Alex sat with that. He thought about how he had imagined a paycheck as a kind of promise, hours converted directly into money, and how the actual thing had a shape he hadn't drawn, with pieces of it routed somewhere he couldn't see, for a future too far off to picture, up to a ceiling he would not reach this year or probably next. Rachelle, when he told her, argued it was theft with extra steps. Emiliano argued it was fine because his grandmother collected a check every month. Alex did not agree with either of them, exactly, and could not yet say what he did believe, only that the number on his next stub would not surprise him, and that this felt, in a small and undramatic way, like being less lied to.

The manager came through the break room carrying a clipboard. "Torres, register three. Alex, you're on popper." Alex pocketed the stub, the small folded paper with its tiny honest column, and went back out to the lobby, where the smell of butter had already found him before he reached the counter.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: A 2001 review titled 'Bad Is Stronger Than Good', led by Roy Baumeister, found that negative events and remarks usually affect people more strongly than positive ones of similar size.
story:
Charles-Antoine came over with his laptop and a bag of his mother's biscotti, the way he always did after a game he wanted to rewatch, and they set up on the kitchen table while Anthony's mother stayed out of the way in the living room. The film was from Saturday, the last match of the season, and Charles-Antoine had played badly in the first half and brilliantly in the second. Anthony had told him this on the bus home: strong on the reset, clever off the blind pass, patient at the breakdown, ruthless in the tackle, and then, at the end, almost as an afterthought, that his first-half positioning had been lazy, that he'd drifted inside and left the wing exposed. Five good things and one bad, roughly. Anthony thought the arithmetic spoke for itself.

Charles-Antoine had gone quiet for the last twenty minutes of the ride, and now, three days later, he picked at the biscotti without eating any of it. "About what you said on the bus," he said, eyes on the screen where his younger self jogged back into position. "The lazy part."

"That was one thing out of six," Anthony said. "You're remembering it wrong."

"I'm remembering the one that mattered."

After Charles-Antoine left, Anthony sat with his own laptop open to a search bar and typed, without quite knowing what he was looking for, why do people only remember criticism. He had planned to introspect properly about it, the way his psychology textbook kept insisting, but instead he skimmed, and an old review came up, from 2001, led by a researcher named Roy Baumeister. The title was blunt, almost rude: "Bad Is Stronger Than Good." Its finding, as far as he could tell from the abstract, was that negative events and remarks usually affect people more strongly than positive ones of the same size. Same size. Not bigger, not more important. The same. He read the sentence twice, then closed the laptop and felt the specific shame of having been accidentally cruel through arithmetic.

He texted Ilan, who had been on the bus too and had heard the whole thing. Ilan replied with a screenshot of the same review and one line: "Told you." Anthony hadn't known Ilan had told him anything, but apparently the observation had been floating around the team for a while, that compliments slid off Charles-Antoine like rain off wax, and that one sharp word lodged in him and stayed. "Bad Is Stronger Than Good," Ilan typed again, as if citing a legal precedent. Anthony put the phone face down.

On Thursday he went to find Mr. Wiśniewski, whose flat was below Anthony's and who had coached youth rugby for thirty years before his knees surrendered. Anthony had reasoned that if the finding was true, then honesty was still required, but the delivery had to change, and he could not work out how to change it alone. Mr. Wiśniewski listened while watering an absurd, florid arrangement of geraniums on his windowsill, and said only, "You watched the film again?" Anthony admitted he had, twice. "Then tell him what you saw, not what you scored."

The distinction took a day to make sense. What Anthony had done on the bus was grade Charles-Antoine, five passes and a fail, and grades of that kind apparently obeyed this lopsided law where the single failure outweighed the rest. What Mr. Wiśniewski seemed to mean was description: this happened, here, at minute twelve, and here is what I'd try instead. Anthony drafted it on paper like an apology he didn't want to cheapen, and tore up two versions for being too florid themselves, too obviously padded with softness around the edges, which he suspected Charles-Antoine would smell instantly.

On Friday Charles-Antoine came over again, ostensibly for biscotti and film, and Anthony waited until the second-half highlights had put him in a good mood. Then he paused the video at minute twelve. "Watch your feet, not the ball," he said. "You step inside, here, because you're reading the fly-half, and that instinct is right nine times out of ten. This was the tenth. The wing was open behind you, and I think if you'd held the wide line one more second, the try comes." He kept his voice even and let the picture do most of the work. Charles-Antoine watched the clip three times, once at quarter speed.

"You're not saying I was lazy," Charles-Antoine said finally.

"I'm saying you guessed wrong once, for a good reason."

Charles-Antoine nodded slowly, and Anthony felt something settle that had been unsettled since the bus, though he still wasn't certain whether this was the real fix or only a better disguise, whether you could ever truly weigh a bad thing against good ones of the same size, or whether all this care just moved the bruise somewhere less visible. Charles-Antoine reached over and restarted the clip, and then, without looking up from the screen, said, "Also, you duck out of contact when the number eight is carrying. Every time. I've been meaning to tell you for two seasons."

The geraniums Mr. Wiśniewski had given Anthony's mother sat on the sill behind the laptop, red and ridiculous, and Anthony looked at them for a moment before he answered. "Show me," he said, and dragged his chair closer to the screen.

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: The term 'unreliable narrator' was coined by the critic Wayne C. Booth in his 1961 book The Rhetoric of Fiction.
story:
Brody had claimed the window seat in the hall nook because it was the only place in the house where nobody expected anything of him until dinner. He had the novel open on his knees, a notebook balanced on the armrest, and his phone face down on the cushion like a witness he intended to ignore. The book was narrated by a man who insisted, in the second chapter, that he had never lied to anyone, and Brody had already counted three lies by page forty.

The problem was the essay. Mr. Do had assigned a thousand words on point of view, and Brody had written half of one sitting here yesterday, the paragraph that used the phrase "unreliable narrator" as if he had coined it himself. It sounded right. It sounded like something a person says when he wants to sound like he has read more than he has. He had lifted it from somewhere, possibly a study guide, possibly a half-remembered class discussion, and now, reading it back, he could not say where it came from.

Linden arrived at four, as arranged, letting himself in through the kitchen the way he had since they were nine. He had his own agenda, which he announced from the hallway: he wanted Brody's opinion on his college essay, the one about his grandfather, which he had revised six times and which he believed was either his masterpiece or a disaster, depending on the hour.

"Read this," Linden said, dropping onto the floor beside the nook with his laptop. "But don't be polite about it. Deegan was polite about it and Deegan is always polite when he's bored."

"Mine first." Brody handed over his draft, watched Linden's eyes travel down the page, and waited for the verdict he already knew was coming.

"Where'd you get 'unreliable narrator'?" Linden said. "Like, is that yours or is that a thing?"

"It's a thing."

"Whose thing?"

Brody looked at the notebook, at the novel, at the window where the afternoon light was doing its diurnal fade toward evening, and did not answer, because the honest answer was that he did not know. "It's a term," he said. "People use it."

"That's not an answer, that's a shrug with vocabulary."

He picked up the phone. It took less than a minute to find, which somehow made it worse, the way finding a thing in a minute makes you feel foolish for not having looked. A critic named Wayne C. Booth had coined the term in 1961, in a book called The Rhetoric of Fiction. Brody read the sentence twice, then wrote it in the margin of his draft, then crossed out the sentence in his draft that had implied the phrase was his own discovery and rewrote it with the attribution inside, where it looked smaller and more honest.

"It was Wayne C. Booth," he told Linden. "Nineteen sixty-one. The Rhetoric of Fiction."

"You looked it up."

"I looked it up."

Linden put a hand over his heart. "Growth," he said, and then turned his laptop around. "Okay, now mine."

Brody read it. It was about a summer at the grandfather's cabin, and in it the grandfather came across as a gentle, wronged saint of a man, which did not match the grandfather Brody had met twice, once at a barbecue where the old man had spent an hour denigrating every neighbour on the street by name. He said none of this. What he said was, "The chronology's weird. You skip the fight and go straight to the lake."

"I skip it because it's not important."

"It's the most important thing that happened and it's not in the essay."

Linden closed the laptop halfway, the screen tilting like a door deciding. "It's a personal essay. It's supposed to show who I am, not catalogue every bad afternoon."

Brody sat with that. He looked at his own draft, at the margin where the crossed-out sentence was still visible beneath the new one, a palimpsest of the exact thing he had just caught Linden doing. Both of them had written narrators who smoothed things over, who left out the parts that made them look small, and both of them had done it so naturally that it had not even felt like a choice. The difference, he thought, was that Booth had a name for it, and Brody had only just learned the name, and he was not yet sure whether knowing the name made him more honest or only better at hiding it.

"Read me the lake part again," he said.

Linden opened the laptop. "It's the part where he teaches me to fish," he said. "It's good. Everyone says it's good."

"Read it anyway."

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Josef Albers made over 1,000 works in his Homage to the Square series from 1950 until 1976, keeping nested squares constant while changing only the colours.
story:
Amy spread her sketchbook across the art room table and counted the pages that mattered. There were four, maybe five, and the portfolio wanted ten. Ten artworks around one theme, plus an artist's statement, due in nine weeks, and all she had so far were drawings of her grandmother's hands, a bus stop in rain, and a jar of pens she'd painted because she couldn't think of anything else.

"You look like someone doing math," said Moses, dropping into the chair across from her. He was already set up, which figured. Moses had known his theme since September: doors, all doors, ten paintings of doorways from the neighbourhood. "What's the problem?"

"I don't have a theme. I have stuff I like." She turned the sketchbook toward him. "My grandmother's hands. That rain one. They don't go together."

"Then pick the hands."

"And do ten more hands? For nine weeks?" She thought of the statement she'd have to write, the paragraph explaining why hands, why ten times. It felt like promising something she couldn't keep.

Moses leaned over and pulled a book from his bag, a fat orange thing she'd seen him carrying around all week. "You know Albers? Josef Albers. Homage to the Square." He opened it to a plate, then another, then another, laying them side by side. Same nested squares in every one, four of them stacked inside each other, and yet the pages felt completely different, some warm as a kitchen, some cold as a swimming pool. "He made over a thousand of these," Moses said. "From 1950 until 1976, when he died. Over a thousand works in the series."

Amy moved the plates around, putting two next to each other that clashed, then a third that made the first two look different again. "Same squares every time."

"Same squares every time. He kept the composition constant and changed only the colours. That's the whole thing. That's all he changed."

She'd assumed, before that moment, that a theme meant a subject. Ten hands, ten doors, ten bus stops. But the squares weren't the subject in the way she'd been thinking about it; the subject was what the colours did to the squares, how the same shape could be sombre or electric depending on what sat inside it. Ten paintings of one thing sounded like repetition to her before. Now it sounded like an experiment. She wasn't sure which it actually was, and she said so.

"It's repetition," Moses said, "but that's not a bad word. He was doing the same thing over and over the way a scientist does." He tapped one plate, rust nested inside grey. "Each one's a result."

Ms. Qureshi came by on her rounds, looked at the Albers book, and asked what they'd found. Amy explained the series herself, the thousand works, the constant squares, the colours as the only variable, and Ms. Qureshi nodded and moved on to the next table without a speech, which Amy appreciated. She'd half expected to be told the idea was derivative, that copying a dead modernist's structure was a shortcut, and she'd been ready to argue that it wasn't copying, it was a method. The argument, unspoken, sat in her chest anyway.

That night she took out her grandmother drawings and looked at them honestly, or tried to. The drawing from memory, done after the hospital, was stiff and careful. The one from the photograph was loose and better and felt like nothing. There was a version of this problem she recognized from elsewhere, from arguing with her mother about whether lighting a candle for her grandmother meant anything or was just something people did because their hands needed occupation. Her mother had said the question was metaphysics, asked in a kitchen, and they'd both laughed, but Amy had gone on wondering. Whether a repeated act gained meaning from the repetition or lost it. Whether ten squares were more than one square or just one square ten times.

She didn't answer it. She got out a fresh sheet and ruled a frame, then nested rectangles inside it, and inside each rectangle she drew her grandmother's hands in a different light: the yellow kitchen bulb, the blue of the television at night, the flat white of the hospital, the orange of a late bus passing the window. The hands stayed the same, positioned the same way, folded the same way. Only the light changed. By the fourth one she could feel the diurnal rhythm of her grandmother's last year moving through the series, morning to night, day into day, without her having planned it that way.

Anne-Sophie found her at lunch the next day, sketchbook open in the cafeteria, and studied the pages upside down. "They're the same drawing," she said.

"The hands are the same drawing. That's the point. It's like Albers."

"Albers?"

"He did a series called Homage to the Square. Over a thousand works in it, from 1950 to 1976. Same nested squares in every one, and he only ever changed the colours."

Anne-Sophie looked at the pages again, longer this time, tilting her head. "It's sad," she said finally. "It's like she's stuck."

The word landed somewhere Amy hadn't expected. She'd been thinking of the constant hands as an anchor, a discipline, and Anne-Sophie had read them as a cage. She turned the sketchbook toward herself and tried to see it that way: her grandmother, unchanging, while the world around her cycled through its lights. Maybe both readings were true at once. Maybe the artist's statement would have to sit with that instead of smoothing it over, and maybe that was the better statement, the honest one. She had nine weeks to find out whether the series would hold together or fall apart, and she knew by now that she wouldn't know until all ten existed.

"Draw me one," Anne-Sophie said. "With her hands holding something. Not just folded."

Amy picked up her pencil and ruled a new frame.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: Mirrors leave blind spots beside and behind a car, so a quick look over the shoulder is needed before merging or changing lanes.
story:
The parking spot outside the bank was the length of a small fjord, narrow and walled in by a van on one side and a hatchback on the other, and Sophie's mother had chosen it on purpose. "Deposit the cheque, then practise the park again on the way out," she said, unbuckling her seatbelt in the passenger seat. "You merge onto the ring road after, and Mr. Nolan said he'd watch from his window and tell you honestly how it looked."

Mr. Nolan was the retired teacher next door who had volunteered his honesty the way other neighbours volunteered zucchini. He had taught her mother's class geography thirty years ago and still described parking spaces in terms of fjords, steep walls, cold water, one careful way in. Sophie had thought the comparison was ridiculous until she tried to reverse into a spot for the first time and understood that fjords were not shaped for anything wider than a small boat.

The test was in nine days. Wassim had taken his the month before and failed on the parallel park alone, and Seamus, who had passed, kept saying it was luck, which was somehow less comforting than failure. "The examiner doesn't extenuate anything," Wassim had told her at lunch, using the word Mr. Nolan had used with them both once, in the old classroom, about how the examiners would not soften their judgments for nerves or bad days. "You either fit in the space or you don't."

Inside the bank, the queue was short. Sophie held her mother's cheque and her learner's permit side by side in her wallet and noticed, in the fluorescent light, how official the permit looked, as though the laminated card had already decided something about her. The teller stamped the deposit without interest. Behind her, a man argued softly about a hold on a cheque, and Sophie listened the way she listened to everything now, testing whether she could hold two thoughts at once, because driving, everyone kept telling her, was exactly that: the hands doing one thing while the eyes did another.

Back at the car, she set up the park. She pulled past the spot, reversed with the wheel turned, watched the van's door handle slide into the frame of her side mirror, straightened, and eased backward until the curb kissed the tyre. She got out and walked around once. Not elegant, but inside the lines. Her mother said nothing, which was the highest available praise.

Then the ring road. The on-ramp rose and curved and the merging lane was short, shorter than it looked from the passenger seat her whole life. Sophie checked the side mirror: empty road, nothing coming. She signalled and began to drift left, and out of the corner of her eye, at her shoulder, a grey sedan sat close enough that she could see the driver's earrings. She pulled the wheel back level, heart working in her throat, and let the car pass. Beside and behind, the mirror had lied to her, or she had lied to herself trusting it; either way, there had been a whole car hidden in the small space between what the glass showed and what was actually there.

"Shoulder check," her mother said quietly, not a scold, just the name for the thing Sophie had just discovered on her own.

"I saw it," Sophie said. "I mean the car. The mirror said empty."

"That's why the check exists."

At the next merge, a kilometre on, Sophie checked the mirror, signalled, then turned her head and looked back over her shoulder into the lane, one full second of the road rushing forward while her eyes faced backward, and the lane was clear, actually clear, and she moved over smooth as a tide. She tried to hold both ideas at once, the way she had practised in the bank queue: the mirror was useful and the mirror was insufficient, and neither of those cancelled the other. Seamus called passing luck; Wassim called failing permanent; her own nascent sense, built one merge at a time, was that the truth lived in the gap between them, in the quick turn of the head that cost a second and saved everything. Whether she could do it under an examiner's clipboard in nine days, she honestly did not know.

They came back down the street toward home, past the bank, past the grey sedan now parked two spaces from her old spot, and Mr. Nolan was standing at his window with both hands raised, thumbs together, measuring the width of an imaginary fjord.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: A 2000 study led by psychologist William Chaplin found that people with firm handshakes tended to make more favorable first impressions.
story:
Mason's grandfather had a grip like a clamp, and he used it every time he wanted to teach something. The night before the hardware store interviews, he shook Mason's hand eleven times in the kitchen, adjusting his pressure each time, until Mason's arm ached and the old man was satisfied. "There was a study in 2000," his grandfather said, still holding on. "Psychologist named William Chaplin led it. People with firm handshakes made more favorable first impressions. More favorable. That's what they found." Mason had laughed, because his grandfather cited research the way other people's grandfathers cited scripture, and because the alternative was to admit his own hand felt like a wet sponge.

At school the next morning, the interviews were being run through the career office, and Mr. Dlamini's classroom had been converted into a waiting area with the desks pushed to the walls. Jaida sat on one of the desks with her application folded into quarters, opening and closing it along the same crease. "I keep thinking if I get the job and you don't, that's fine, and if you get it and I don't, that's also fine," she said. "But neither of those things feels fine."

"They're hiring four people," Mason said. "It's not either of us."

"Tell that to my stomach."

Kyleigh came in holding a printout of interview questions she'd found online, and she appointed herself examiner. She pulled two chairs to the front of the room and made Mason sit while she read questions in a flat, official voice that kept cracking. Why do you want this job. What are your strengths. Where do you see yourself in five years. Mason answered each one to the window, because the window was easier than her face.

"Eye contact," Kyleigh said. "The whole point is eye contact."

"I'm looking at you."

"You're looking at my forehead. It's different."

He tried again, holding her gaze the way you'd hold your breath underwater, and the strange thing was that his answers got worse, not better. They came out shorter, stiffer, as if some part of his brain had been diverted to the business of not blinking. Behind them, Mr. Dlamini was grading papers at his desk and pretending not to listen, though Mason had noticed him underline something on his page whenever the handshake business came up, which it did, because Mason had told the story twice already, once for Kyleigh and once for a boy he didn't know who was also interviewing and had asked why Mason kept flexing his right hand.

"My grandfather wants to inculcate the firm handshake before three o'clock," Mason said. "He's very committed to it."

"What's inculcate," the boy said.

"Beat it into me," Mason said. "Basically."

Mr. Dlamini looked up then. "My father was the same way," he said, and did not add anything else, which Mason found almost worse than a lecture, because it meant the condition was hereditary and global and there was no cure.

The problem, as Mason understood it by lunch, was that he was being trained by two incompatible philosophies. His grandfather's method was mechanical: firm handshake, studied in 2000 by a psychologist named Chaplin, who found that firm handshakes made more favorable first impressions, therefore squeeze. Kyleigh's method was theatrical: eye contact, clear answers, performed confidence, as if the interview were a scene she could rehearse until the rehearsal vanished. His grandfather thought you could build an impression from the outside in. Kyleigh seemed to believe the opposite, that the outside would follow if the inside cooperated.
