Mason sat in the cafeteria turning his water bottle and could not decide which of them was right, or whether they were both right about different things, or whether the truth was that some people walked into rooms and other people rehearsed walking into rooms and the rooms could tell the difference.

His grandfather was irascible about most topics, taxes and traffic and the neighbor's leaf blower, but about handshakes he was serene, certain, patient. That certainty had its own authority. Mason kept thinking about it during fifth period, that a man who had shaken hands for sixty years and a study from 2000 had arrived at the same conclusion, while Kyleigh, who had never interviewed for anything, had arrived at a different one by way of a website. Neither of them had actually been in the room where the decision would be made.

By the time his name was called, at 3:40, he had settled on something that was not quite either position. He would shake the manager's hand firmly, because there was no cost to it and a study had found what it had found, and he would look at her while he did it, and he would answer the questions as well as he could, and he would not pretend to know whether the impression came from his hand or his eyes or something underneath both that he could not rehearse. He did not feel certain. He felt like a person holding two tools he only half trusted.

The manager's office smelled like pencil shavings and rubber matting. She was smaller than he expected and she stood to greet him. He offered his hand, and she took it, and her grip was firmer than his grandfather's. "Mason," she said, reading his application. "Tell me about yourself."

"My grandfather taught me to shake hands last night," he heard himself say. "Eleven times. In the kitchen."

She laughed, still holding his hand, and Mason held on and looked her in the eye.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: After a concussion, athletes return through graduated steps from rest to full play, moving to the next step only while they stay free of symptoms.
story:
Luke had been the one who talked Angelo's little sister onto the team in the fall, telling the coach she could trap a ball better than half the returning midfielders, and he had been the one standing ten feet away in the October game when she went up for a header, got undercut, and landed wrong. He remembered it in fragments now, the way memory edited without permission: the sound the crowd made, the trainer's hand hovering near her shoulder, the long walk she made to the sideline alone while play restarted around her.

She came back to practice three weeks later, cleared by a doctor Luke never saw, and for two sessions she looked like herself, sharp and quick to laugh. Then came the Wednesday drills. Light stuff, jogging lines and short passes, nothing anyone would call contact. Halfway through the second set she stopped at the cone, put two fingers against her temple, and walked off toward the bench without asking permission. Mr. Campbell, who coached the boys in the fall and helped with this team in spring, jogged over, and Luke, close enough to hear because he'd been slacking on his own footwork, caught her saying the headache was back.

"Then you don't move up," Mr. Campbell said. "You drop back a stage. Rest first, then light work, and you only step forward again if you stay free of symptoms the whole way through."

She argued, briefly, in the flat voice people use when they know they've already lost. Luke pretended to be very interested in his laces.

Afterward, in the parking lot, Angelo pushed his bag into the trunk and said, "She's furious. She thinks sitting out makes her soft." He didn't say the other thing, the thing about Luke's header against Riverside last season, so Luke didn't say it either, and the silence between them had a familiar shape, like a room they'd both agreed not to enter.

Because there had been a moment, in that Riverside game, when Luke took an elbow and the field went white at the edges, and he had stayed on. He had even scored, afterward, a clean finish off a cross from Rylan, and everyone had treated the goal as proof he was fine. Rylan still brought it up at lunch, laughing. Luke had learned to laugh too, to verbalize nothing about the two days of headaches that followed, the curtains drawn in his bedroom at noon. At the time it had seemed like toughness, the ordinary price of the season. Now, watching Angelo's sister sit on the bench with her hood up while the rest of them ran shooting drills, toughness looked less like a virtue and more like a veneer, a thin coating he'd been polishing since he was twelve because it got him picked first.

He thought about that on the drive home and hated how tidy it sounded, like a poster in a gymnasium. His older cousin had played through everything and never regretted it, and there was something real in that, too, some old idea about obligation to the people depending on you. Both things felt true. He couldn't make them sit still together.

Thursday he found her before practice, spinning a ball on one finger near the equipment shed. "How's the head," he said, and it came out like an accusation, so he tried again. "How are the stages going?"

"Back to the rest one," she said. "Then light drills again. Doctor says I move up one at a time, only if nothing comes back. If I get symptoms, I go back down." She was matter-of-fact about it now, almost bored, which surprised him. "It's slower than getting injured in the first place. That's the stupid part."

"Riverside," Luke said. The word sat there. He hadn't planned to say it, and once it was out he understood he'd been carrying the sentence around for months the way you carry something in a coat pocket, forgetting and rediscovering it. He told her about the white edges, the two days of headaches, the goal. He did not dress it up as wisdom. He told it the way it happened, including the part where everyone cheered.

She stopped spinning the ball and looked at him with something he couldn't read, an affective flatness that he suspected concealed more than it revealed, and then she said, "You scored, though."

"Yeah," Luke said. "I scored."

He couldn't tell whether that was the point or the whole problem, and he was still deciding when Mr. Campbell blew the whistle across the field and she handed him the ball, tucked her hands in her sleeves, and walked back to the bench to start the count again.

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: In England, a tenancy deposit is capped at five weeks' rent when the annual rent is under 50,000 pounds, and at six weeks' rent when it is 50,000 pounds or more.
story:
Megan spread the two printed leases across the kitchen table, one on either side of the fruit bowl, the way other people might lay out tarot cards. The flat on Haldon Road wanted eight hundred and forty pounds a month plus a deposit of nine hundred and seventy. The one behind the launderette on Princes Street wanted seven hundred and ninety, but its utilities were not included, and its deposit was listed as one thousand two hundred. Her mother had said, before leaving for her shift, "Pick the one that's actually cheaper, not the one that looks cheaper," which Megan had taken as permission to spend the whole evening with a calculator.

She had learned to compare leases the way Mr. Tran had shown the class in the spring, back when it had seemed like an abstract exercise: monthly rent, then utilities, then any compulsory fees, then the deposit divided across the months of the tenancy to get a true picture of what moving in would cost. In England, he had told them, tenants pay a deposit at the start, and there are rules about how big it can be. He had written nothing on the board except the word "deposit" and underlined it, which at the time had seemed like a stunt and now seemed like the whole point.

Foster arrived at seven with two energy drinks and a laptop, having texted "did you seriously ask me over to do maths." He sat down anyway, pulled the Haldon Road lease toward himself, and began reading aloud in the voice of a bored lawyer. Megan let him get through half a paragraph before she raised a hand to forestall the performance. "Look at the deposit lines first," she said. "Both of them. Something's wrong with one of them and I can't tell which."

Foster found the government page on his laptop while Megan worked the arithmetic by hand, because she trusted her own handwriting more than a screen she couldn't annotate. The rule was simple once she saw it: a tenancy deposit in England is capped at five weeks' rent when the annual rent is under fifty thousand pounds, and at six weeks' rent when the annual rent is fifty thousand pounds or more. She read it twice, then again, then said it out loud to Foster so it would stick. "Five weeks under fifty thousand a year. Six weeks if it's fifty thousand or more." Haldon Road's annual rent came to ten thousand and eighty, well under the line, so its ceiling was five weeks. Seven hundred and ninety was also under the line, and therefore also capped at five weeks.

She calculated five weeks of the Princes Street rent by dividing seven hundred and ninety by four and multiplying by five, then cross-checking with a weeks-in-a-year method that gave the same answer, nine hundred and eighty-seven pounds and fifty pence. The lease was asking for one thousand two hundred. She checked it a third time using a different order of operations, as if the number might change of its own volition, and it did not. The landlord behind the launderette was asking over two hundred pounds more than the cap allowed. "That's not a rounding error," Foster said, leaning in. "That's two hundred quid."

The Haldon Road deposit of nine hundred and seventy, by contrast, sat just under its own limit of one thousand and fifty. Megan felt a strange, embryonic satisfaction, the feeling of a skill that had not yet hardened into anything she could claim, but that had for the first time produced a result in the world. She wrote both deposit ceilings in the margins of the leases and circled the overcharge on Princes Street twice.

But when she went back to the utilities, the picture tilted. Princes Street included nothing: no water, no electricity, no internet, and the letting agent's notes estimated bills at a hundred and ten a month. Haldon Road covered water and internet but not electricity, and it was fifty pounds a month dearer in rent. On total monthly cost including utilities, Haldon Road came to about nine hundred and ten and Princes Street to about nine hundred. The cheaper-looking flat was, by a hair, actually cheaper, if the estimate held, which was exactly the part Megan could not verify. Estimates were not leases. Bills in winter were not bills in June. She wrote both totals at the bottom of the page and stared at them, wanting one to be clearly wrong so the decision would make itself, and neither one obliged.

She could report the deposit overcharge, or mention it in her email to the agent and see whether the number shrank, which would tell her something about who she was dealing with. Or she could walk away and let someone else find it. Megan pulled the calculator toward her again and started dividing the Princes Street deposit by twelve, to see what it would do to the true monthly cost even if the agent agreed to drop it to the cap. Foster cracked his second energy drink and watched her write. "You're going to be one of those people who reads the whole contract," he said. She didn't look up. "Five weeks," she said, "under fifty thousand a year. Write that on your hand."

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: India has marked voters' fingers with indelible ink based on silver nitrate since its 1962 general election, so no one can vote twice.
story:
The photograph arrived on Annabelle's phone at seven in the morning, while she was still in her pajamas eating toast. Her cousin Priya, who lived in Delhi, stood squinting in the sun with one finger held up like a small flag, and the fingertip was stained a deep, unmistakable purple-black. Priya had captioned it with a row of exclamation points and the words "third time!" Annabelle had stared at the mark, at the unbothered pride on her cousin's face, and wondered what kind of ink survived handwashing, showers, a week of ordinary living. She sent back a single question mark and finished her toast.

By lunch she had the answer, or most of it. Nash, who sat behind her in civics and seemed to absorb stray facts the way a sponge absorbs spillage, leaned over her phone. "That's the election ink," he said. "India's marked voters' fingers with indelible ink since its 1962 general election, so no one can vote twice. It's silver nitrate." He shrugged and returned to his sandwich as if he had said nothing remarkable, but Annabelle kept turning the words over. Silver nitrate. Indelible. She liked the weight of it, the way one small mark could settle a question that otherwise stayed open forever.

She was sixteen, two years too young for anything but opinions, and the opinion she held that afternoon was that the junior class council election, scheduled for Friday, was going to be a mess. Last spring the ballots had been loose slips of paper in a shoebox, and everyone agreed, in the aggrieved way of people who enjoy agreeing, that certain individuals had voted more than once. The results had been equivocal, to say the least; Devan had lost the treasurer spot by three votes and had spent a week doing mock funerals for democracy at the lunch table.

On Thursday afternoon Annabelle and Devan and Nash took over the corner table at the coffee shop on Miller Street, where the window fogged from the espresso machine and Ms. Xu, their neighbor, graded essays two tables away with a red pen and a cappuccino. Annabelle spread out her notebook. "Here's my proposal," she said. "Everyone dips a finger in the ink pad before they get a ballot. One finger, one vote. If you've already got the mark, you don't get a slip."

Devan frowned at the ink pad she'd bought with her babysitting money, a stamp pad from the craft store labeled non-toxic and washable. "Washable," he said. "So after one trip to the bathroom, I'm a fresh voter again."

"That's the flaw," Annabelle admitted. She turned her own hand over and looked at her clean fingers. "Priya's stain lasted more than a week, and that's silver nitrate, which we can't exactly get at the craft store. So we have the right idea in the wrong phylum." Nash laughed at that, and she flushed, pleased. "But it doesn't have to last a week. It only has to last until Friday afternoon. Nobody votes again after the box closes."

They tested it. Nash pressed his index finger onto the pad, shook the resulting smudge under soap in the coffee shop bathroom for a full sixty seconds while Devan timed him, and came back holding up a finger that had faded to a ghost of itself but not vanished. "Equivocal," Devan said. "I can't tell if that counts as marked or not." Annabelle leaned in, considering. Under the fluorescent light, a violet shadow clung to the whorls of Nash's fingerprint, and she thought that a tired volunteer at the end of a Friday might call it clean.

"What if we double-dip?" Nash asked. "Two coats. And what if the volunteer has the list too, and crosses off names?" Annabelle wrote both ideas down. She was aware, dimly, of how strange it was to feel so excited about redundancy, about a system built on the assumption that people would try to cheat. It did not augur well for the human race, maybe, but it augured quite well for Friday. From two tables away, Ms. Xu looked up from her essays. "I've been listening," she said, "because you're loud. The Elections Commission would like your notebook." She held out her hand for it, smiling, and Annabelle passed it over and watched her teacher read, chewing the cap of the red pen.

The election went through without a single contested ballot. The ink was craft-store ink and it washed off by Sunday, but it held its color through Friday, and forty-three purple-smudged fingers signed yearbooks that afternoon. Devan won treasurer by eleven votes and insisted on inspecting every marked hand himself, like a customs officer. That evening Annabelle texted Priya a photograph of her own hand, index finger stamped and raised against the coffee shop window, the streetlight behind it going soft through the fog on the glass.

Priya wrote back within a minute: "What election?"

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The 2026 FIFA World Cup, hosted by Canada, Mexico and the United States, was the first with 48 teams and the first hosted by three countries.
story:
The living room smelled of burned cheese and lime, because Tristen had been put in charge of the nachos and Mr. Bautista had arrived carrying a pot of tamales still steaming through the towel wrapped around it. Brianna sat on the arm of the couch with the best view of the television, a position she had earned by arriving first, and around her the room filled: her father in his recliner, Blake sprawled on the rug with a bowl he refused to share, Tristen shuttling between kitchen and coffee table. On the screen the stadium in Monterrey was a wash of green and white, the crowd noise rising and falling like something tidal.

"This is the biggest one ever," Blake said, gesturing at the screen with a tortilla chip. "That's why it feels different. Everything about it is bigger."

"It's the same as always," Tristen said from the kitchen doorway. "Thirty-two teams, same as every tournament since forever. You're just feeling it because we're hosting."

"It's not thirty-two," Brianna said, mostly to see what would happen.

Both of them turned. Blake narrowed his eyes the way he did in debate class, when he was about to build something out of nothing. "It's thirty-two. Everyone knows that. Name one thing that's different."

Brianna could not, actually, name one thing. She remembered a headline, a number that had seemed absurd at the time, and she remembered her cousin talking about tickets in Vancouver, and she remembered that this tournament kept being called a World Cup of three flags, but none of it had assembled itself into anything she could defend. "I just remember it being more," she said. "I could be wrong."

"You are wrong," Tristen said, but without conviction, because Tristen's convictions ran out quickly when they were tested.

Mr. Bautista set the tamales down and lowered himself into the corner of the couch, the seat her mother usually took, which her mother had surrendered to him with visible ceremony. He was their neighbor from two doors down, retired, the owner of the loudest lawn mower on the street, and tonight he wore a green jersey so new it still had fold lines across the chest, as though he had tried to burnish the whole occasion by dressing for it. "It's not thirty-two," he said. He said it quietly, in the tone of a man holding a card he was deciding whether to play.

"See," Blake said. "Wait. Which is it, not thirty-two?"

"Tell them," Mr. Bautista said to Brianna. "You were there when I told your father."

She had not been there, or she had been in the hallway and heard only fragments, but she pulled out her phone anyway. Halftime was eleven minutes away, and Tristen had already declared that the argument had to be settled before the second half kicked off, because he refused to watch the rest of the match with a disputed fact hanging over the room like weather. The screen's glow caught the edges of the tamales' husks, and her father asked whether anyone was going to actually eat them or just admire them, and the page loaded slowly, the way pages always load when everyone is watching you.

Forty-eight teams. She read it twice. She scrolled and read it again, and there it was, plain as the score at the top of the screen: the first World Cup with forty-eight teams, hosted by Canada, Mexico and the United States, the first ever hosted by three countries. "Forty-eight," she said. "It's the first one with forty-eight teams. And it's the first time three countries hosted it together. Canada, Mexico, and us."

The room rearranged itself around the number. Tristen said forty-eight was too many and that it cheapened the thing, and Blake said more teams meant more games like this one, and her father said the travel alone must be brutal. But Mr. Bautista had gone still in the corner of the couch, and when he spoke it was not about the number at all. "Three countries," he said. "Everyone says America's World Cup. I keep waiting to hear the other two." He picked up a tamale and turned it over in his hands without opening it. "My brother in Guadalajara keeps count. Every time they say only the American cities, he texts me the tally."

Brianna watched him, and she understood that he had not come for the food or even the football, or not only. He had come because his team was on the screen in his jersey and he wanted the room to hold all three of those flags, not just the nearest one. She thought of Blake, who wanted to be right, and Tristen, who wanted the argument closed by halftime so he could enjoy the match, and she thought about how a fact could be true and still be only a fraction of what mattered. In school they had called the appeal of facts logos, the cold clean machinery of argument, and she had liked that machinery, trusted it. But forty-eight was true, and three countries was true, and none of it said anything about a man alone in a living room keeping count for his brother.

"I'll count with you," she said. "The announcers, I mean. When they say all three countries, we tally that too."

Mr. Bautista looked at her for a moment, and then he opened the tamale. "You count the ones they leave out," he said. "That's the number I want."

On the screen the halftime whistle blew, and the room filled again with talk, and Brianna reached for a tamale and set her phone face-up on her knee, the tally app open and waiting.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: The Seder plate holds maror, bitter herbs such as horseradish, which are eaten to recall the bitterness of slavery in Egypt.
story:
Charlie had never noticed how loud the kitchen got until it was hers to run. Her mother was at the sink pretending not to hover, her grandfather had claimed the chair nearest the stove, and the smell of chicken soup had taken over the room the way weather takes over a sky. On the counter lay the Seder plate, still empty, its small hollows waiting like an argument waiting to be made.

"You're sure you don't want me to do the order of it," her mother said, not quite a question.

"I'm sure." Charlie lined up the dishes she had prepared over three evenings: the charoset, the shank bone borrowed from a neighbor, the egg she had boiled and scorched, and the horseradish root she'd grated herself until her eyes streamed and she had to stand at the window to recover. The bitterness in the air had outlasted the grating. It clung to the cutting board and would not leave.

The doorbell rang before she was ready. It was Cale, who lived two streets over and had said yes when Charlie invited him last week, mostly because he'd asked what a Seder actually was and she'd found she couldn't summarize it in a hallway. He came in holding a box of matzah like it might break, which, she supposed, it might.

"Nobody in my family does anything like this," he said, hovering at the edge of the kitchen. "Christmas, and that's it. My grandma makes a ham."

"You'll be fine," Charlie said, and then, quieter, "I'll be fine. First time running the whole thing. Usually my mom does it and I just read the part about the four questions." She was still acclimating to the idea that everyone at the table would be watching her tonight, waiting for cues she wasn't certain she could give.

Her grandfather watched from his chair. "Your grandmother ran it for thirty years," he said. "She had it down like a machine. Every machination timed. Soup on at the second syllable of the blessing." He smiled at the plate. "You'll be sloppier. Sloppy is fine."

Charlie didn't answer. She set the horseradish in its place on the plate and looked at it for a long moment, because it was the item she had thought about most all week. The matzah was poor bread, the charoset was mortar, the egg was grief or rebirth depending who you asked, but the bitter herb had unsettled her when she was small and still unsettled her now. She had asked her mother once, years ago, why they did that to themselves on purpose, on a night that was supposed to be about freedom, and her mother had said, "You'll understand when you lead it." Which had felt like an evasion then and felt like something else now.

They moved to the table. Cale sat between Charlie and her grandfather, twisting his napkin. Hafsa, Charlie's closest friend since seventh grade, sat across from him, back for her third Seder at their house, comfortable enough now to steal an olive before anything official began. When Charlie lifted the first cup and stumbled through the opening blessing, her voice steadier than she expected, her mother caught her eye and nodded once, quickly, and looked away.

It went mostly as planned until the maror. Charlie held up the plate so everyone could see the pale grated root, and Cale leaned toward it, frowning. "I have to eat that? On purpose? It smells like a fight."

"It's called maror," Charlie said. "Bitter herbs. Horseradish." She kept the plate level. "We eat it to recall the bitterness of slavery in Egypt."

Cale stared at her. "You eat something terrible so you remember something terrible."

"That's the part I used to hate," Hafsa said, dipping her karpas in the salt water like a veteran. "When I was little I thought, we're free, why do we need the horseradish? My dad said ask a better question."

"And did you?"

"I decided the better question was, what's it like to not need it. And I couldn't answer that either."

Charlie handed each of them a piece of matzah with maror on it, and her grandfather took his without ceremony, and her mother took hers, and then it was Cale's turn. He held it at a slight distance, the way a person holds a dare.

"I came tonight because you said it would be interesting," he said. "You didn't say it would hurt."

"Only for a second," Charlie said. "And that's kind of the point. I've been thinking about it all week. I always figured remembering bad things was something you couldn't avoid, so why schedule it. But maybe it's the opposite. If you choose the moment, it's yours. If you don't, it just kind of ambushes you." She heard her grandfather shift in his chair and realized she was thinking out loud in front of everyone, which she would not have done a year ago. "I'm not sure that's right. I'm still working on it."

Cale ate his piece. His eyes watered immediately, and he gripped the table with both hands, and Hafsa laughed so hard she nearly dropped her own maror, and Charlie's grandfather said, "Now you know," and reached over to thump Cale on the back like a man starting a stubborn engine. Cale drank half a glass of water and then, still streaming, still grimacing, held out his cup for more horseradish.

"Wait, again? You hated it," Charlie said.

"Yeah," he said, wiping his face. "But it's the first thing all year that everyone at a table did at the same time, on purpose, and meant it." He took a second piece and waited, eyes narrowed, for her to pass the matzah.

Charlie looked at her mother, who shrugged, and at the plate in her own hands, and at the empty hollow where the maror had been. She got up, went back into the kitchen, and returned with the cutting board, the grater, and the last knuckle of horseradish root, which she set down in front of Cale.

"Then you're doing the next one," she said. "Everyone watches the leader. That's how it works."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Isaac Newton arranged the colors of the spectrum into a circle in his 1704 book Opticks, an early version of the color wheel artists use today.
story:
The kitchen table had been Abigail's studio for three days now, which meant her mother had been remonstrating about the glitter in the butter dish for roughly the same length of time. Abigail spread her swatches across the wood like a fortune-teller's cards: teal, marigold, a violet so dark it looked like a bruise. The assignment was a self-portrait in a color scheme of her choosing, due Friday, and Ms. Thompson had said, with that acerbic tilt she used when she wanted you to feel clever, "Choose your palette like you'd choose your friends. On purpose."

"You're staring at those like they owe you money," said Mahelie, who had let herself in through the back door the way she always did, and was now eating cereal dry out of the box.

"I'm staring at them like I don't know what I believe in yet." Abigail slid the teal next to the marigold and immediately regretted it. "Complementary colors, right? Opposites on the wheel. Blue and orange. That's the safe answer, that's the answer everyone gives, and I would rather die than hand in the same portrait Aryana hands in."

"Aryana's doing complementary."

"Aryana found out what complementary meant on Tuesday and hasn't stopped announcing it since."

Mahelie sat down across from her, hugging the cereal box to her chest with a possessiveness that Abigail noted but chose, for the moment, to ignore. Mahelie's own portfolio was empty. She'd spent the whole term drawing nothing, claiming she was "in a conceptual phase," which everyone understood to mean she was frightened. That was the subtext of every visit to Abigail's kitchen table: Mahelie wanted a scheme she could borrow, a plan someone else had already tested, and she wanted it without having to ask out loud.

"You know what I found out at like two in the morning?" Abigail pulled her phone from under a tube of cadmium red and turned the screen around. "The color wheel. It wasn't invented by a painter. Isaac Newton arranged the colors of the spectrum into a circle. It's in his book Opticks, from 1704. A physicist made the thing we all use to pick paint."

"Newton? Apple guy?"

"Gravity guy, prism guy, apparently also color-wheel guy." Abigail traced the circle on the screen with her fingertip. "So all weekend I've been thinking it's basically an ontology. Like, a whole system for what colors even are, and which ones are opposites, and it didn't come down from a mountain. Some man bent light through a prism and bent it into a shape."

Mahelie leaned over the box, and a single cornflake fell onto the violet swatch. "So you're saying the wheel is made up."

"I'm saying it's made. By a person. Which is different." Abigail fished the cornflake off the violet and ate it, because principles only went so far. "Ms. Thompson said pick a scheme on purpose. So maybe the purpose isn't picking the correct one. Maybe it's picking two that shouldn't work and making them work."

She took the teal and the violet, the two colors she'd been keeping apart because they were cousins, not opposites, because there was no tension in them, and set them side by side anyway. Then, on a scrap of watercolor paper, she dragged a streak of the marigold through the middle like a fault line. It shouldn't have worked. It did, a little, the yellow cutting the two cool colors open so they glowed at the edges.

"Oh," said Mahelie, very quietly.

"I know."

"Can I..."

Abigail looked up. Mahelie had the box clutched so hard the cardboard had buckled, and her face had gone the particular pink of someone about to ask for something enormous disguised as something small.

"You can borrow the violet," Abigail said, "but not the scheme. The scheme's mine. The scheme is the whole point." She pushed the scrap of test paper across the table, the one with the fault line in it. "Start here. Newton bent light into a circle and called it a day. You can bend somebody's idea into your own. That's allowed. That's basically the entire history of art."

Mahelie took the scrap with both hands, the way you'd take a bird. "I'm going to do a portrait of my grandmother," she said, "in violet and marigold and whatever that third one is."

"Teal. And that's very close to borrowing the scheme."

"It's an homage."

"It's grand larceny," said Abigail, but she was already taping fresh paper to the table, already squeezing the violet onto the palette, and when her mother came in to remonstrate once more about the glitter, Abigail picked up the brush, dipped it in the marigold, and made the first cut.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: The genetic code is read in codons of three bases; there are 64 possible codons but only 20 standard amino acids, so most amino acids have more than one codon.
story:
The codon chart was taped to the fume hood at a slight angle, and David had already straightened it twice. Ms. Pritchard had given him until Friday to explain transcription and translation properly, out loud, in her lab after last period, or the unit mark would stand. He had written, on the quiz, that the cell needed sixty-four different amino acids because there were sixty-four codons. She had circled it in red and written one word: "Come see me."

"You're overcomplicating it," Manreet said, dropping her bag on the counter beside his. She had stayed behind without being asked, which David had learned not to comment on. "You always do this. You memorize the shape of the answer instead of the answer."

"I memorized the chart wrong." He slid his notebook toward her, where he had gridded out the bases in fours, assuming each combination meant something distinct. "Four bases, three at a time. That's sixty-four. So I figured, sixty-four codons, sixty-four amino acids, one for one."

Manreet tapped the chart with two fingers, right over the column for leucine. "Count the codons there."

He counted. Six. He moved to serine and counted four, then arginine and counted six again, and his ears went warm. "There are only twenty amino acids," he said slowly. "The standard twenty. So most of them have more than one codon."

"There you go."

"So the code repeats itself." He said it as though confessing to something. "All that precision, and it says the same word six different ways." Behind Manreet, above the sink, a faded poster of a Norwegian fjord leaned its grey water against the wall, left over from when the geography teacher had used this room, and David stared at it while the idea settled. The cliff walls were exact; the water filled whatever space they left.

Manreet watched him work, chin on her fist. She had her own quiz to fix, a paragraph on RNA polymerase she had bungled by being too casual, writing "the enzyme does its thing" and hoping for charm marks. It had not worked. But watching David was different, because David did not get things wrong through carelessness. He got them wrong through a kind of ambition, building towers where a bridge would do. She had known him since grade nine, when he had argued with a supply teacher about whether mitochondria were technically alive, and she had liked him for it even though he had lost.

Jasper arrived at the door with two vending machine cookies and the demeanour of someone who thinks attendance is support enough. "Pritchard still in her office?" he asked.

"Five minutes," Manreet said.

"Good, because I need to tell you about my weekend before you go in there and become a scientist." He set a cookie beside David's notebook. "My uncle has decided we're kayaking a fjord in July. A fjord. I told him I get seasick in the bath, and he said the water's basically flat, which is exactly what a pugnacious man says before he tips you over."

"Flat water in a deep trench," David said, not looking up. "The walls do the work." He was still running his finger down the chart, verifying, codon by codon, that the redundancy held everywhere, not just in the columns he had checked. Somewhere between alanine and valine he stopped feeling cheated by the repetition and started feeling steadied by it. Sixty-four possible codons, twenty standard amino acids, most amino acids with more than one spelling. The cell could tolerate a sloppy letter now and then and still build the right protein. That was not a flaw in his understanding; it had been a flaw in his assumption that nature kept one word for one thing.

When Ms. Pritchard came in carrying her mug, David's throat tightened, but he stood anyway and walked to the whiteboard.

"Transcription first," he said, and drew the strand, the messenger RNA peeling off it, then the ribosome moving along with its three-base codons. At the part that had sunk him before, he did not flinch. "The code is read in codons of three bases," he said. "There are sixty-four possible codons, but only twenty standard amino acids, so most amino acids have more than one codon." He pointed at the chart. "Leucine has six."

Ms. Pritchard sipped her tea and wrote nothing, which he chose to read as exoneration. Then she said, "Now explain why that might matter to the organism."

David looked at the chart, at the water in the poster, at Manreet, who raised one eyebrow.

"I can get it wrong," he said, "and still get it right."

"Say more."

"A wrong base doesn't always change the protein." He paused. "Sometimes. Not always. I don't know the full story of when it matters yet."

She set the mug down. "Friday. Same time. Bring me the rest."

Jasper broke his cookie in half and held a piece out to David. "So does this mean you're a scientist now, or do you still have to pass?"

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: Doubling the size of a sorted list adds only one extra step to a binary search, while it doubles the worst-case work of a linear search.
story:
The robotics team's parts list had grown to four thousand entries overnight, and Adam found out because the lookup on the club laptop took so long that Eileen had time to eat half a granola bar before the part number appeared on screen.

"That's new," she said, crumbs on her keyboard. "It used to be instant."

Ms. Goh had given them two functions to compare at the start of the term, back when the list was two thousand entries: a linear search that walked the list from the front, and a binary search that kept cutting the list in half. Adam's job at today's coding club meeting was to demo both and explain which one a sorted list deserved. He had assumed the answer. He had even rehearsed a small speech about it. Now the speech seemed to portend something awkward, because the slow function on screen was the one he had privately rooted against, and it was embarrassing himself in public.

He ran the binary version on the same four thousand entries. The result came back before the Enter key had finished clicking.

"Did it even do it?" Eileen leaned over his shoulder. "Check again."

He checked again. Same instant. He ran it ten times, then ran the linear one ten times, timing each with a loop counter they had built for exactly this comparison. The slow one was doing, at worst, twice the work it had done on the old list. The fast one had gained exactly one extra step.

"One step," Sylvie said from across the room, where she was cataloguing resistors nobody would ever use. "You doubled the list and it cost you one step. That's not fair to the other function. Someone should file a complaint on its behalf."

"Its main detractor is me," Adam admitted. "I called it the dumb one in my notes. In writing."

Sylvie came over, dragging her chair, and made him run the old list size again so she could see the numbers side by side. Two thousand entries: the binary version took a certain number of steps, the linear version took up to two thousand. Four thousand entries: the binary version took one step more than before, the linear version took up to four thousand. She wrote the numbers on the whiteboard with a purple marker, then underlined the single added step twice, hard, as if it owed her money.

"So when Coach says the list might double again before regionals," Sylvie said, "the dumb one gets twice as slow again, and this one buys one more step. One."

"That's the whole pitch," Adam said. "I don't have to say it's elegant. I just show the board."

Ms. Goh circled the tables the way she did, hands behind her back, radiating a policy of never answering anything until you had suffered appropriately first. She looked at the whiteboard for a long moment. "Who labeled these functions?"

"Adam called one of them the dumb one," Eileen said promptly. "In his notes. He confessed voluntarily. Sort of."

"The linear search has one advantage you haven't mentioned," Ms. Goh said, which was the closest she came to mercy, and then she moved on before Adam could ask what it was.

He thought about it while disassembling last year's demo robot, which had a bad habit and deserved it. The linear search worked on any list, sorted or not. The binary one only worked because someone had done the boring work of putting the parts in order first. So the fast function wasn't free; it stood on top of a choice somebody else had made, and if that someone ever got lazy and appended new parts to the end of the file, the binary search would quietly return wrong answers, instantly, with total confidence. He tested it. He appended one resistor to the end of the sorted file, ran the binary lookup, and watched it report, in microseconds, that the resistor did not exist.

"Okay," he said out loud. "It's fast and it's wrong. That's a combo."

"It's not wrong, it's opinionated," Sylvie said. "Like you, about the dumb one."

For the demo, Adam rebuilt the talk in his head. He would show the two timings on the doubled list, the linear one doing twice its worst-case work, the binary one paying a single extra step, and then he would point at the appended resistor and admit that the speed depended on the sorting, and that he hadn't checked the sorting until ten minutes ago. Honesty as a feature, not a bug. He rehearsed the opening line twice under his breath while Eileen pretended not to listen and graded his delivery with her eyebrows.

At the end of the meeting, three younger members who had never spoken to him before came over to ask which function they should use for their own project. Adam, feeling briefly sagacious, told them it depended on whether their list was sorted, and whether they could promise it would stay sorted, and whether they wanted to be fast or merely right. They thanked him and wrote nothing down.

The next morning Eileen texted him a screenshot. The parts list had doubled again overnight, to eight thousand entries, because the coach had found a surplus sale. Every lookup he ran on the binary version came back in the same blink as before, one step richer than the day before, unbothered, serene. The linear version, which he had insulted in writing and then spent an hour defending the honor of, now took so long that he could have eaten a whole granola bar. He sat looking at the two timings side by side, then reopened his notes and, above the words "the dumb one," typed a small correction: "the honest one, when nobody sorts."

His screen dimmed before he could decide whether to delete it.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: Braking distance is proportional to the square of speed, so doubling a car's speed makes the distance needed to brake about four times as long.
story:
Hailey had spent the whole bus ride to the licensing office impugning the entire process: the booklet, the eye test, the woman at the counter who said "next window, please" like a recording. Her mother had insisted she was ready, and her friend Noa had texted that morning to say driving was easier than parallel parking a shopping cart, which Hailey found neither accurate nor comforting. Still, she had passed the written test, and the permit sat in her back pocket, stiff and official, so when the clerk pointed to a door marked Behind-the-Wheel Lessons, she went through it.

The car waited in the subterranean garage under the building, a gray sedan with a second brake pedal bolted in on the passenger side. The instructor was Ms. Khoury, who lived two streets over from Hailey and had once coached the middle-school soccer team, which meant she already knew exactly how badly Hailey handled pressure. "We start in the garage," Ms. Khoury said, handing over the keys. "You drive out. Slow is a skill, not a consolation prize."

Hailey started the engine, checked the mirror she'd been told to check, and eased the car up the ramp into daylight. The streets behind the office were wide and nearly empty, one of those mid-morning stretches when the city seems to be holding its breath. She was doing fine, actually, until Ms. Khoury asked her a question.

"Say you're going thirty and you need forty feet to stop," Ms. Khoury said. "You double your speed to sixty. How many feet do you need now?"

"Eighty," Hailey said, and then, sensing from the pause that this was wrong, "a hundred?" The horn of a delivery truck behind them made her grip the wheel. In her head she heard Ziad from physics class, who had once tried to explain something about squares on the whiteboard while she drew in the margins of her notebook. She hadn't listened then. She tried now, halving and doubling in her head, and felt the answer arrive like something she'd dropped and found again. "Four times. A hundred and sixty feet." Braking distance, Ziad had said, goes up with the square of your speed, so doubling your speed makes the distance you need to brake about four times as long. She'd written it on a quiz and gotten it right and then buried it, the way school knowledge went subterranean and stayed there until a Tuesday morning on a quiet street pulled it back up.

"Better late than never," Ms. Khoury said, which Hailey would have taken as condescension a week ago, from any adult, especially one her mother approvingly called a born pedagogue. Today it sounded like something else. Ms. Khoury leaned forward and pointed at the speedometer. "So now tell me why you're doing forty-five in a school zone."

Hailey lifted her foot. She watched the needle sink, thirty, twenty-five, and then, half a block ahead, a yellow ball rolled off a driveway followed by a small dog with no leash and no apparent fear of cars. Hailey braked. Not a slam, though every nerve wanted a slam; a firm, early press, because a number she had gotten wrong once and then right was sitting in her head telling her exactly how long a gray sedan takes to stop from twenty-five. The car settled to a halt six feet from the dog, which sniffed the tire, decided the machine was beneath its notice, and trotted back up the driveway after its ball.

For a moment neither of them spoke. Hailey's hands were shaking on the wheel and she was grinning in a way she couldn't have stopped if she'd wanted to. "I'd have hit it at forty-five," she said. "Wouldn't I."

"I don't run that experiment," Ms. Khoury said. "But the arithmetic doesn't lie, and neither do tires." She settled back and looked out at the street as if the near miss had been an item on a checklist, checked. "Turn left at the light. We'll take the long way back."

Hailey signaled, checked the mirror, and turned, smooth enough that she felt it in her whole body. She was still uncertain about plenty: highway merges, the width of the car, whether courage or caution was supposed to win when they argued. But she understood something she hadn't that morning, that the rules she'd resented on the bus weren't fences put up by people who thought she was stupid. They were arithmetic, written down by people who had done the stopping-distance experiment the hard way, with skid marks. She drove the long way back, steady at the limit, and when they pulled into the subterranean garage Ms. Khoury said, "Same time Thursday. Bring your questions."

"Can I bring the dog a treat?" Hailey said, and cut the engine.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Kwanzaa, created by Maulana Karenga in 1966, runs from December 26 to January 1 and honors seven principles, one each day, beginning with Umoja, meaning unity.
story:
Justine arrived at the park pavilion carrying the kinara her grandmother had entrusted to her, wrapped in a dish towel because the felt lining had gone missing sometime in the last eleven months. The tables were already filling: her aunts unfolding card tables, her father arguing cheerfully with an uncle about where the speakers should go, small cousins chasing each other around the barbecue pit even though nobody was cooking in it. December 26th, first night, and this year her grandmother had decided the whole celebration would happen outdoors, in the public park by the river, because the house had gotten too small for the family it had to hold.

"Justine," her grandmother said, catching her sleeve before she could set down the kinara. "You're explaining the principle tonight. First night. You're eighteen now, old enough."

"Explaining it how?" Justine asked, though she knew how. Every year someone stood at the front table and talked about the day's principle for a few minutes, and every year Justine had watched from the back, half listening, half scrolling. She had assumed she had years before it would be her turn.

However she pleased, apparently, because her grandmother had already moved on to instruct an aunt about the fruit bowl.

She found Eunice and Oceanne at the edge of the pavilion, the two of them perched on the picnic table like birds who had agreed to attend this event only if they were permitted to observe it ironically. Eunice had known Justine since fourth grade; Oceanne had transferred in junior year and had attached herself to both of them with a loyalty that felt sometimes like a compliment and sometimes like surveillance.

"You're doing the speech," Oceanne said. It wasn't a question; she had heard the grandmother.

"It's not a speech. It's like three minutes."

"Same thing," said Eunice. "You'll be great. You're the perspicacious one." Justine couldn't tell whether this was sincere or a joke at her expense, which was the usual condition of Eunice's compliments.

The problem was that Justine did not actually know the first principle. She knew there were seven, knew the holiday had started in 1966, that a man named Maulana Karenga had created it, that it ran from December 26 to January 1, one principle for each day. Her grandmother had drilled all of this into her over the years the way she drilled multiplication tables, so that the facts sat in Justine's head whether she wanted them or not. But the principles themselves had never inured themselves to her the way the dates had; the names slid off every time she tried to hold one.

"Look it up," Eunice whispered, when Justine confessed this.

"On my phone, in front of Grandma."

"She'll never know."

Justine knew she would know. Her grandmother noticed everything, had once deduced from the angle of Justine's chin that she was lying about finishing a book report. But she also could not stand at the front table in an hour and say nothing. Two ways of doing this tugged at her: the quiet way, the phone under the table, a fact smuggled in and passed off as knowledge; and the honest way, which was to find her grandmother, admit the gap, and be taught like a child in front of everyone.

She chose a third way, which was to go find Ms. Park.

Ms. Park was the retired music teacher who lived two houses down from Justine's grandmother and who came to the celebration every year, uninvited and entirely welcome, bringing a container of something nobody else would have thought to bring. This year it was sesame candy. She was arranging it on a paper plate when Justine found her.

"Ms. Park, do you know the first principle? The first night's principle?"

Ms. Park looked at her for a long moment, then at the kinara still under Justine's arm, then back. "What do you know already?"

"It starts today, December 26, and goes to January 1. Seven days, seven principles, one each day. Karenga created it in 1966." The list came out flat and complete, an annuity of facts her grandmother had deposited year after year, paying out now whether or not Justine had ever earned it.

"And the word for the first one?"

"That's what I'm asking."

"I'm not going to give you something you can hand over like a receipt," Ms. Park said. "Ask your grandmother what it means to her. Then you'll have something worth standing up with."

Which was, Justine understood, exactly what she had been avoiding. She found her grandmother by the river railing, alone for once, looking at the water going gray in the late light.

"Grandma. I don't know the first principle's name."

Her grandmother did not look surprised, and somehow that was worse than a scolding. "Umoja," she said. "It means unity."

"Just that?"

"It means all of this," her grandmother said, and gestured at the pavilion behind them, the aunts, the cousins, the cousins' friends, Eunice and Oceanne sitting at the edge of it all pretending not to belong to it, Ms. Park's sesame candy already being picked over. "It means I can put all these people in one place and they stay."

When the aunt rang the bell and the family gathered, Justine stood at the front table with the kinara and lit the black candle in the center. She said the name, umoja, and what it meant, and then she said what she had worked out on the walk back from the railing: that unity was not the same as agreement, that half the people in that pavilion were not speaking to the other half, that they came anyway. She said she had not known the word an hour ago and had had to ask, and she watched her grandmother's face do something complicated at that, pride and grief occupying it at once.

Afterward Oceanne hugged her and Eunice said, "See, perspicacious," and Justine laughed and did not correct her, because the truth was she had not been clever at all; she had only, finally, asked. She carried the kinara back to her grandmother's car wrapped in the dish towel, one candle burned down a little further than the rest, and the river behind the pavilion still moving, dark, carrying whatever it carried toward the first of January.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: In Judaism, the closest relatives of the person who died sit shiva, a mourning period of seven days that begins after the burial; the Hebrew word shiva means seven.
story:
The casseroles started arriving before the burial was over. Tristan counted four on the counter by the time the family got back, and his mother kept moving them to make room, rearranging the kitchen like a proof she couldn't quite finish. His grandfather had died on Tuesday, quietly, in a hospital Tristan hadn't managed to visit that last week because of finals, and now it was Thursday and the house was full of people Tristan half knew, and his chemistry textbook was still open on the table to a chapter on enthalpy, of all things, as if the universe had a sense of humor he didn't appreciate.

"Someone should move your book," his aunt said, not moving it.

"Chem final's Monday," Tristan said. It sounded like an excuse even to him. Enthalpy, he could define it perfectly: the total heat content of a system, measured under constant pressure. He had written the definition on a flashcard. The flashcard was somewhere under a dish of kugel.

The mirrors in the house had been covered with cloth that morning. Tristan had watched his father do it, draping a bath towel over the hallway mirror with the kind of care he usually reserved for the good china, and Tristan had not asked why, because asking would have meant admitting he didn't know, and he'd spent seventeen years not admitting that. His grandfather had been the religious one, the one who read and argued and could pontificate for a full hour about a single line of Torah while Tristan ate his grandmother's noodle soup and waited for the arguing to become dinner conversation again. Tristan had always assumed there would be more time to ask him things.

Bradley showed up at six with Faris, both of them standing in the doorway of the kitchen holding a plastic container of cookies like it was a live grenade. Tristan had texted Bradley the address and nothing else. Faris looked at the covered mirrors, at the low chairs his father and aunt were sitting on, at the paper announcement taped to the cabinet that read SHIVA in block letters, and leaned toward Tristan.

"What's shiva?" Faris asked, quietly.

"It means seven," Tristan's mother said from the low chair, before Tristan could answer. She smiled a little, the first time since Tuesday. "Seven days of mourning, after the burial. We sit and people come."

"Oh," Faris said. "So, like, you're on day one."

"Day one," his father confirmed.

Bradley set the cookies down on the counter between two casseroles, and then the three of them stood there, and Tristan understood suddenly that they were waiting for permission, that they didn't know what to say any more than he would have known at their kitchen table. "You can sit," Tristan said. "That's mostly what it is. People sit."

They sat. Faris asked about the low chairs and Tristan admitted he didn't know, and his aunt said something about grief keeping you low to the ground, and Tristan didn't know if that was the real reason or her own invention, and he let it stand, because the not knowing had stopped feeling like a failure somewhere around the second hour. His grandfather, he suspected, would have known, would have had sources, would have argued the point until the noodle soup went cold. The loss of that was its own specific shape, separate from the loss of the man.

Mr. Ramírez from next door came by with a lemon cake and stayed forty minutes, mostly reticent, which Tristan found restful after a day of relatives narrating their grief at him. Mr. Ramírez had taught Tristan to solder when he was eleven and had played chess with his grandfather on Sundays for a decade. He asked Tristan if he wanted a game later, and Tristan said yes, and meant it, and noticed that his mother, across the kitchen, had stopped rearranging things and was just sitting, holding a cup of tea someone had made her without being asked.

Around eight, Bradley pulled the chemistry textbook out from under the kugel dish and slid it across the table. "You said the final's Monday," he said. "I brought my notes. Enthalpy's like half the exam." Tristan looked at the notes, dense and messy in Bradley's handwriting, and then at his grandfather's photograph, which someone had propped on the windowsill next to the seventh-day candle his aunt had lit with a match she kept cupping against the draft.

"Tomorrow," Tristan said. "Not tonight."

"Tonight's for sitting," Faris said, and Tristan nodded, because that was exactly right, and because there were six more days, and because on Monday there would be enthalpy, systems and their heat, and he would carry what he could from one to the other.

His mother touched the back of his neck on her way past, and he moved the book aside and cut Bradley's cookies onto a plate.

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: A linear search checks items one by one from the start, so in the worst case, when the target is last or missing, it must look at every item.
story:
The bell for last period had already rung, and Andrew was still staring at the cursor blinking at the bottom of his screen. The file of student names, all 4,382 of them, sat in memory sorted alphabetically, and his program was supposed to find any name in it. It found the ones near the top of the alphabet quickly enough. But when he typed a name that was not there at all, the program hung, the little hourglass spinning, and Mr. Charles stood behind him with his arms crossed.

"Your demo is in ten minutes," Mr. Charles said. "For the whole class."

"I know." Andrew's voice came out flat. He watched the hourglass spin. A minute. Two.

Evelyne leaned over from the next terminal. "Try searching for Aardvark." He did. Instant: not found. "Now try Zylstra." He typed it. The hourglass again. "It's the last or missing names, isn't it," she said. "The ones at the end of the alphabet."

Andrew scrolled his own code. It was a loop, and the loop was honest: start at the first record, compare, move to the next, compare again. It checked items one by one from the start, and it did not stop until it had looked at every single one. A missing name meant the loop ran to the very end of the file, 4,382 comparisons, and the machine did each one with the patience of a clerk who had never heard of skipping. "So the worst case is when the name is last or not there at all," he said slowly. "Then it has to look at every item in the file. That's why it crawls."

"That's a linear search," Evelyne said.

"That's a charlatan of a search," Alan said from across the lab, not looking up from his own machine. "It pretends to work. It works for Aardvark."

Andrew laughed despite himself, then stopped laughing, because the clock on the wall said he had nine minutes and Mr. Charles had already begun pulling the projector screen down. He thought of his father, who ran a hardware store and had once shown him how to find a part number in a catalog: you never started at page one. You opened the book in the middle, decided whether your number came before or after, and threw half the book away. His father's hands doing it, quick and sure, the way he did everything. Andrew had watched without really watching, the way you watch a parent, and only now did the memory loosen itself from where it had calcified into just another afternoon.

The file was sorted. That was the whole point. It was sorted and he was searching it as though it were a pile of laundry.

He opened a new file and started typing. Set low to the first index, high to the last. Find the middle. Compare. If the target comes before the middle, throw away the top half; if after, throw away the bottom. Evelyne pulled her chair over without asking. "What's that doing?"

"Cutting the problem in half," Andrew said. "Every time. One comparison and half the file is gone. Then again, and again."

Alan drifted over too, chewing the end of a pen. "So how many comparisons for the whole thing?"

Andrew didn't answer right away, because he didn't want to guess and be a charlatan himself. He counted it out on his fingers instead, halving and halving. Somewhere around twelve. Twelve versus 4,382, in the case that mattered, the missing name, the name at the end. He said the numbers out loud and heard Alan stop chewing.

The bug took six minutes to find, and it was small and stupid: he had used the wrong comparison operator, so when the target equaled the middle name exactly, the loop threw away the half containing it and then searched forever in a half where it could never be. Evelyne spotted it. "There," she said, tapping the screen. "Equal. You're not handling equal."

"Two minutes," Mr. Charles said.

Andrew fixed it, compiled it, and his hands were not quite steady on the keys. He typed Zylstra. The screen answered before the hourglass could even form: not found. He typed a name from the middle of the alphabet, found it, and then, because there was no time to be careful about it, a name that was not a name at all, Xqqqsmith. Not found, instantly, and it felt almost profligate, that speed, like spending something he hadn't earned.

The class gathered. Mr. Charles stood at the back with his clipboard, and Andrew ran the old version first, on purpose, searching for Zylstra while everyone watched the hourglass turn and turn. Someone in the back said, "It's frozen." Then he killed it, ran the new version, and the answer appeared so fast that a few people laughed, the way you laugh at a magic trick you didn't catch.

"How," said a girl near the front.

Andrew looked at the sorted list on the screen, then at Mr. Charles, who had raised one eyebrow but said nothing, leaving the floor entirely to him. "The old one checked every record from the start, one at a time. If the name was missing, it looked at all of them before it could say so. This one cuts the file in half with each comparison, because the file is sorted, so half of it can never contain the answer anyway." He paused. "It only works on sorted data. That's the trade. If the data weren't sorted, I'd have to check everything, and this would be worthless."

Evelyne raised her hand as though it were still a classroom and not a demo. "So which is better?"

"That depends on what you're willing to pay," Andrew said. "To sort, or not to sort. I don't have the whole answer to that yet."

Mr. Charles made a small mark on his clipboard, and behind him the projector fan hummed into the quiet. Andrew clicked the search bar one more time and typed his own name.

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: Canada's federal Goods and Services Tax, introduced on January 1, 1991 at 7 percent, has been 5 percent since January 1, 2008.
story:
Michael had forty-one dollars in his bank account, a paycheque coming Friday, and a 1994 Corolla with a For Sale sign on it two blocks from the restaurant, priced at nine hundred. He had until Saturday. He knew this because he had walked past the car four times since Tuesday, once with Rio, who had leaned on the hood until the owner came out and told him to lean on his own car.

Friday night he worked the counter at the Lantern, a Thai place with six booths and a kitchen that sounded like a argument that never fully ended. His paycheque came in an envelope because the owner didn't trust computers, and Michael opened it beside the register between orders. He read the stub twice. Gross pay: $412. Then a column of deductions that took bites out of it, income tax and CPP and EI, each line small and certain, until the net pay at the bottom said $372.51.

"Thirty-nine dollars gone," he said to Rio, who was refilling the napkin dispenser because it looked like work and Mr. Sok, the owner, paid Rio in spring rolls to do small jobs Rio mostly invented.

"Tax man cometh," Rio said. "My dad says welcome to the rest of your life. He files his return in March and yells at the ceiling."

Mr. Sok came through with a tray, dour as always, gray apron, the face of a man who had seen a thousand Friday nights. "Napkins don't need a supervisor, Rio."

"My plan needs a supervisor." Rio had been planning, all week, to convince Mr. Sok to let him run a social media account for the restaurant, which mostly meant photographing his own food. "I'm a content creator in development."

"You're a napkin creator in development."

Michael slid his stub back into the envelope and took a booth's order, pad out, and the woman asked what the total would come to with tax, and he said he'd have to ring it in to know. When her receipt printed, he stood at the register and looked at the lines: subtotal $28.50, GST $1.43, PST $2.85, and the total below. He did the math on the pad's back. The GST came to five cents on the dollar.

He frowned at it. Behind the register, taped inside the shelf where the pens lived, was an old yellowed receipt Mr. Sok kept for some reason no one had ever asked about. Michael had looked at it during slow shifts, the way you look at anything within reach. It was from this same counter, dated January 1991, before Michael was born. At the bottom, under the subtotal, the GST line was seven percent. He'd assumed, all this time, that was the rate. That was the tax. Seven on every dollar, forever, since the beginning.

"Megan," he called to the doorway, where Megan was waiting for her pickup order and reading the menu she had memorized months ago. "You're good at math. What's the GST now?"

"Five percent," she said. "It's been five since January first, 2008. My mom complains about it every April." She tilted her head. "Why, what did you think?"

He turned the yellowed receipt around so she could see it. "This says seven."

She came closer, read it. "That's the year it started. New Year's Day, 1991, seven percent." She said it the way she said most things, as though the facts were lined up somewhere waiting for her. "So it dropped. In 2008."

Mr. Sok passed behind them with the tray again. "That receipt is my first week open," he said, and kept walking.

"Then it's an indictment of my education," Michael said. "I've been checking that thing for a year."

"Of your attention span," Megan said, and took her bag of food.

Rio leaned in, phone already out. "This is content. A restaurant so old its receipts are artifacts. Mr. Sok, think about the engagement."

"Think about the windows," Mr. Sok said, pointing at the ones Rio was supposed to wipe.

Michael rang up the next customer and watched the GST appear, five percent, small and lawful, and thought about his own deductions on the stub, the government taking its share on both ends, the money he hadn't earned yet already spoken for. He counted what he had: this cheque net, plus tips in the jar, plus the forty-one, minus what he owed his mom for the phone bill. He might make the nine hundred by Saturday. He might make it by Sunday, and the car might be gone.

When the counter cleared he took his tips to the back and counted them under the light by the freezer. Rio appeared in the doorway, wiping his hands.

"Mr. Sok says I can post one photo," Rio said. "One. I'm starting an empire."

"Start it with a rag," Michael called, and pushed through the kitchen doors with the money in his fist.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: Most US employment is at-will, meaning the employer or the worker can end the job at any time for any reason that is not illegal.
story:
Christian filled out the paperwork at the returns counter of Hendricks Supply while the register drawer clattered open and shut behind him. Ms. Moose, who owned the store and had interviewed him in the aisle between pipe fittings and caulk, slid a pen across the counter without looking up from her ledger. He was eighteen, he had no experience except mowing lawns, and he wanted the job for reasons he had not fully dichotomized in his own mind: money for the fall, yes, but also something harder to name, the sense that a place might expect him somewhere at a certain hour. His mother had said, that morning, that it was good he was starting small. His father said nothing, because his father's office had let him go in March and the word "starting" had gone strange in their house.

He read the form before signing it, which surprised him, because he was the kind of person who usually skimmed. Near the bottom, above the signature line, a paragraph stated that employment was at-will, meaning the employer or the worker could end the job at any time for any reason that was not illegal. He read it twice. The phrase had a clean, mutual sound, like a handshake, though something in it also felt like standing on ice.

"Nobody ever reads that part," Ms. Moose said, taking the page from him. "You can quit tomorrow if you hate it. I can let you go tomorrow if you're terrible. Fair's fair." Then she handed him a smock with HENDRICKS stenciled on the chest, one size too large, smelling of the previous wearer's cigarettes.

His phone buzzed while he was learning the key cutter. It was Maeve, who had wanted him to apply at the bookstore with her and had taken his defection personally.

"Tell me the truth," she wrote. "Did you take it because of the pay or because you're scared of the bookstore being boring? Because I got a callback and I need to know if I'm about to spend a summer alphabetizing poetry alone." He typed that the pay was better, deleted it, and typed instead: "They can fire me whenever they want. I can leave whenever I want. It's called at-will. It felt honest." Then he watched the cutting wheel throw sparks, feeling he had sent something both true and evasive, a small betrayal of how much he wanted her to say she'd stay at the bookstore either way.

The third hire was Emilee, who had just finished her first year at the state college and spent the slow afternoon hours explaining to Christian that she was only there to save for a car, a Civic, silver if possible, and that she had already begun to dichotomize her savings into "car money" and "escape money," though she admitted the categories kept leaking into each other. When a customer asked for help matching a paint chip, she abandoned him mid-sentence, and Christian stood alone beneath the fluorescent lights with a chip the color of jaundiced cream, unsure whether his job included the paint counter at all. He matched it anyway, by eye, and the customer thanked him, and he felt the strange private weight of a thing done competently with no one watching.

The twist came on his ninth shift, in the form of a scheduling note taped to the time clock. Ms. Moose was cutting summer hours; the store had lost the contract with the apartment complex that bought its locks in bulk. Emilee's shifts were halved. Christian, lowest on the ladder, was kept on, and when he asked why, Ms. Moose only said that the last kid before him had walked out on a Saturday with no notice, ten customers deep, and she had decided she would rather keep the one who read the fine print. The gain sat badly in him, though he took the hours. At the bus stop afterward he texted Emilee, and she replied with a single message: "Silver Civic postponed. I'll get it eventually. Don't feel weird, you read a paragraph, I didn't." He did feel weird. He read the message four times on the ride home.

His father found him at the kitchen table that night with his pay envelope, the first of his life, flat and unremarkable in its smallness. His father picked it up, weighed it in his hand like a coin of uncertain denomination, and set it back down. "They can let you go anytime," Christian said, not quite knowing why he was saying it, whether as warning or comfort. "That's how it works. The other way too." His father looked at him for a long moment, and what crossed his face was not bitterness exactly, something more like recognition, and he said, "I know how it works," and went to the sink and washed his hands for a long time.

Maeve started at the bookstore on a Monday. Emilee picked up weekend shifts at the garden center across the highway and saved in smaller increments toward the same car. Christian kept working the key cutter, and on the last Saturday of June he cut a key for an old man who had locked himself out of his house, and the old man tested it against the store's demonstration lock, and it turned on the first try, and the old man grinned at him with whole uncomplicated delight. Christian grinned back, and behind them the door chimed, and Ms. Moose called from the register, "Christian, customer up front," and he untied and retied the smong at his waist and went.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: Psychologists call it misattribution of arousal when a racing heart caused by fear or excitement is mistaken for attraction to the person nearby.
story:
Nathan had rehearsed the opening line twice in the car, and both versions had sounded better alone. Now he stood in the doorway of Starlight Lanes holding his own shoes in a plastic bag, watching Sonia pick a ball from the rack, testing its weight the way she had once explained in physics class: not by lifting it but by rolling her wrist, letting the object tell her what it was. He had liked her since February, in a slow, accumulating way, like lint. She hadn't noticed, or had noticed and let it sit, which was its own kind of answer he hadn't learned to read.

"Rental's on you," she said, sliding her card across the counter before he could reach his wallet. "Winner pays for nachos."

The first game they split, not deliberately. Nathan rolled a gutter ball and laughed at himself loudly enough to cover the flush climbing his neck, and Sonia answered with three strikes in a row, shrugging as though her hands belonged to someone else. Between frames she told him about her cousin's wedding, where an uncle had made a toast so long that the ice sculpture melted. Nathan listened and bowled and listened, and noticed that whenever she leaned over the ball return to say something quiet, his heart went strange and percussive, like something caged behind his ribs being let out for exercise.

Her friend Aurora arrived halfway through the second game, not bowling, just perched on the sticky orange seat with a lemonade, narrating. "He's throwing it too flat," she announced to the lane at large. "You want lift, Nathan. You're bowling like you're mad at the pins." He was not mad at the pins. He was trying to appear composed while a girl he liked watched his posture from four feet away, which turned out to be a difficult thing to do with a twelve-pound object in his hand. He bowled worse. Sonia bowled worse too, glancing over at him mid-approach, and Aurora kept score with theatrical gasps, and by the tenth frame they were tied, 127 to 127, and a tiebreaker was declared.

That was when Mr. Tan, the neighbour who ran the pro shop and came out on Friday nights to fix the pinsetters, paused beside their lane with a rag over his shoulder. "Tense game," he said, not a question. He watched Sonia line up her shot. "You kids are all shaking. Like it's the Olympics." He laughed at his own observation and moved on toward lane six, dragging his rag along the ball return as he went.

The tiebreaker frame took forever. Sonia needed a mark; Nathan needed her to miss, which he felt immediately ashamed of wanting. Her ball hooked wide, clipped the seven pin, and wobbled the ten down in a slow, reluctant second strike. The noise was enormous. Aurora screamed. Sonia turned around with her fists up, and there, under the black lights, her white shoelaces glowing violet, Nathan felt his own heart slamming and a hot, bright certainty flood him: this, right now, her, exactly this.

He bowled his frame in a kind of haze, got nine, lost, and paid for nachos with hands that would not entirely steady.

In line at the snack bar, Sonia was looking at him differently, or he was looking at everything differently, or both, and he tried to introspect his way through it, which was a habit his mother called his worst one. His heart was still racing. His palms were damp.
