And then he remembered a podcast Aurora had played on the bus in the spring, something about a bridge and an experiment, and he heard again the voice saying the phrase that had stuck to him like a burr: "Psychologists call it misattribution of arousal." He had looked it up that night, alone, and now the whole idea came back to him with an unpleasant click: a racing heart caused by fear or excitement can be mistaken for attraction to the person nearby. He had just lost a tiebreaker. His body was full of adrenaline and noise. Was the bright certainty about Sonia, or about the ten pin?

Sonia watched Nathan go quiet in the nacho line, his mouth slightly open, and she wondered what was happening behind his eyes. He did that, went somewhere internal, and usually she found it interesting, but tonight it felt like a door closing on something she had been circling all evening. She had bowled badly on purpose for two frames and didn't want to examine why, so she didn't. She tapped his arm. "Penny for them," she said, pointing at his thoughts. He started to say something, stopped, and visibly decided against a version of it.

"It's nothing," Nathan said. "Good strike, though." He carried the nachos to the table, and the cheese had already begun to set around the edges, and Sonia sat down across from him and stole the first chip.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: At a Chinese New Year's Eve reunion dinner, fish is traditionally served because the word for fish, 'yu', sounds like the word for surplus or abundance.
story:
I had the menu finished before my grandmother even asked, which is why I didn't understand why she kept saying no. She'd handed the reunion dinner to me this year, the whole thing, the temple hall booked for our family on New Year's Eve, the incense and the rice and the order of the dishes, and she'd done it with a little ceremony of her own, pressing the shopping list into my hand like a subpoena, like something I was legally required to answer for. So I answered for it. Steamed chicken, long noodles, the dumplings she and I fold every winter break, eight vegetables because eight is lucky and because I could actually get eight good ones from the market by the temple. I left the fish off. Fish is a pain to carry on two buses, it stinks up the kitchen at the hall, and half the little cousins pick around it anyway.

"No," my grandmother said, in the temple kitchen on Sunday, tapping the list with one finger. "The fish stays."

"Ba, it's one dinner. I've got it covered."

"The fish stays, Jordyn."

She can be stubborn, my grandmother. She once refused to speak to an aunt for three years over a card game, and when I was nine I decided that this was the same thing, some old rule I would never be told the reason for. I figured I could cajole her out of it, or simply out-organize her, because that's what she'd been training me for all along, obviously. That was my read on the situation. She wanted to see whether I could hold the whole dinner in my head, and I could, minus one smelly fish.

Billie, who'd come along to help haul the ingredients because Billie always comes along, was leaning against the counter eating the candied lotus root she was supposed to be portioning into bowls. "Just put the fish on the list," she said, nonchalant, like it cost her nothing, though I noticed she'd been angling all afternoon to be given a real job, something bigger than lotus root, and she thought agreeing with my grandmother might get her promoted to the dumplings. "It's one more dish."

"It's one more dish I have to carry on the 47 bus."

"Then Jared and I will carry it." She said it too quickly. That was the other thing about Billie this winter, the way she kept volunteering for things she'd never cared about, the early mornings, the heavy lifting. I assumed it was about the credit, about being able to say she'd helped lead something. I was very sure of my assumptions that day. That's the part I keep coming back to.

I went to find my grandmother in the main hall, where she was wiping down the long tables and arguing softly with Ms. Nielsen, the temple's caretaker, about how many folding chairs the back room actually held. Ms. Nielsen said forty, my grandmother said sixty, and my grandmother was winning the way she always won, by simply continuing to speak. I stood beside her with the list and waited for my moment, and it came when she stopped to catch her breath, which had been coming shorter all month, though she'd told me it was nothing and I'd told myself I believed her.

"Ba, tell me why it matters," I said. "The fish. You never make it any other night."

She looked at me for a while, long enough that Ms. Nielsen quietly took the rag and started on the far table.

"Yu," my grandmother said. "The fish. It sounds like the word for surplus, for abundance. You leave some on the plate at the end, so there's more next year. Your grandfather taught me that one." She picked up her rag again. "It cannot be left off."

I could have argued that half our family doesn't believe in luck, that my father calls it all superstition and still eats more than anyone, that plenty of things get left off every year and nobody starves for it. I could have argued that a word sounding like another word isn't a reason, it's a pun, and I don't build menus on puns. And underneath all of that I was still sure this was a test of my competence, that the fish was a bargaining chip in some game between us. It took me until we were locking up, until I watched her count the chairs twice in the doorway and lose her place the second time, to understand that it might not have been about me at all. She was handing me the dinner and holding on to one dish the way you hold on to a railing. Or maybe that's me making it neat after the fact. I don't actually know which it was, and I've decided I can live without knowing.

I called Billie from the temple steps. "Add the fish to the list," I said. "And you're on dumplings. With me, not under me, so stop looking at me like that."

"I'm not looking like anything," Billie said, but she was grinning, and I could hear it.

"Whole fish," I said. "Jared's car. And we leave some on the plate."

"Leftovers on purpose," Billie said. "My grandmother would faint."

On New Year's Eve, when the cousins were loud and the steam had fogged the windows of the hall, I set the fish in the center of the table with its head pointed toward my grandmother, because I'd asked Ms. Nielsen which way mattered and she'd shrugged and said whichever way the eldest person is sitting. My grandmother looked at the fish, then at me, and didn't say anything, which from her was a paragraph. At the end of the night there were two pieces left on the platter, silver and untouched, and she reached over with her chopsticks and moved one of them half an inch, so it lay straight.

"Good," she said. "Now there's some left."

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Milk chocolate is usually tempered to a lower working temperature than dark chocolate, around 29-30 degrees Celsius, because milk fat softens the cocoa butter.
story:
The thermometer read 45 degrees when Amelia lowered it into the bowl, and her grandfather tapped the glass with one finger as though it might be persuaded to lie. He had handed her the bag of milk chocolate couverture that morning without ceremony, the way he handed over most things, and said only, "The double boiler is under the sink." She had wanted to learn all summer, since the June afternoon he'd snapped a bar of his dark chocolate over the kitchen counter and it had broken like glass, clean-edged and shining, and she had understood in a small, sharp way that she wanted to make something do that.

He had explained the method once, in his way, which meant fragments. Two thirds of the chocolate melted, he'd said, then the rest stirred in off the heat, "seeding" it, and you worked it until it cooled, testing a smear on the back of a spoon. He worked almost exclusively with dark chocolate, 70 percent, and the temperatures he kept in his head were dark chocolate temperatures. Amelia did not know there was a difference. She stirred and watched the surface begin to undulate in slow, satiny waves, thickening as the couverture cooled, and at 32 degrees, per the numbers he'd given her, she dipped the spoon and waited.

The smear stayed wet. After five minutes it was still tacky, dull, stubbornly refusing everything. Her grandfather came in from the garden, looked at the spoon, looked at the thermometer, and said nothing, which in his language was a kind of accusation. Amelia felt it anyway, the unfairness of doing everything she'd been told and getting nothing.

"That's not right," she said. "I did it exactly."

"Obviously not," he said, and washed his hands.

She texted Sameer, who worked weekends at a chocolate shop across town and owed her for covering his chemistry homework in June. Sameer replied fast, as he always did when he got to be the expert. wait. milk or dark? Amelia typed milk. He sent a single laughing emoji, then: dark temps won't work. milk chocolate goes lower, like 29 30. She stared at the numbers, then at the thermometer, which had drifted down to 30 on its own, and realized the batch was, for the moment, exactly where it needed to be and she hadn't known it. She grabbed a spoon.

"Because of the milk fat," Sameer's next message said. "Milk fat softens the cocoa butter."

She smeared a new test on a fresh spoon and held her breath. Mr. Flores, the neighbour, chose that moment to appear at the screen door with a jar of his own honey, which he traded annually for chocolate in an arrangement he called, with total seriousness, their fiduciary relationship. Amelia had once tried to explain that fiduciary meant something more specific than that, and he had waved her off. He leaned over the counter now, peering at the spoon.

"It's setting," he said. "Shiny. You see that shine?"

"I see it," she said, and she did: the smear had gone from wet to matte to a faint polish in under a minute, firming with an almost audible authority.

Her grandfather came back with mud on his shoes, and Amelia held up the spoon before he could speak. "Milk chocolate. You have to take it lower than dark, down around 29, 30 degrees." He took the spoon, turned it over, pressed one fingernail into the edge. It held. He set it down.

"Milk," he said, as though she had told him the oven was an epicurean conspiracy against him. "Who buys milk chocolate."

"You do. It's in your cupboard. Kayden's been stealing it since eighth grade, ask him."

He grunted, but he pulled a bowl toward himself and began scraping the thickened chocolate off the sides, folding it back through, which was as close to an apology as his hands knew how to make. Amelia had spent an hour believing the failure was hers, some flaw in her patience or her stirring, and now she understood it had been a translation problem, his numbers carried from one chocolate to another like a map of the wrong country. She wasn't sure which bothered her more: that he hadn't known, or that she had assumed he must.

She poured the tempered milk chocolate into the bar mould and tapped it flat against the counter, the way he did, twice on each side. They waited together, not speaking. Mr. Flores ate a spoon of honey.

When the bar came out, she snapped a corner off and it broke clean, with a sound like a small, decisive door closing. She put the piece in her grandfather's palm and watched him put it in his mouth.

"Lower," he said finally. "All right."

She was already melting the next batch, thermometer in her left hand, and reached to turn the heat down without looking.

activity: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
knowledge_domain: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
fact: A 2013 study led by John Cook examined 11,944 climate paper abstracts and found that 97.1 percent of those taking a position endorsed human-caused global warming.
story:
The bus smelled of someone's smuggled chocolate croissants, and Nathan had spent the two-hour ride arguing with Matilda about whether their chemistry teacher counted as an epicurean for bringing a thermos of single-origin coffee on a school trip. He lost that argument on the outskirts of the university town, where the lab building rose out of the frost like a filing cabinet somebody had left out overnight. Mr. Horváth counted them twice at the door, as though the parking lot might have swallowed one of them.

Inside, a graduate student in a faded conference t-shirt walked them past rooms full of equipment Nathan wanted to touch and was not allowed to touch. In the third room, a man sat hunched over a spreadsheet so wide it spilled across two monitors, and Nathan, drifting at the back, read a column heading upside down: abstracts coded. He asked what the column was for. The man, clearly grateful for any interruption, said he was checking someone else's numbers before the paper went out, because if his numbers didn't match, the whole thing got sent back.

"That seems inefficient," said Bria, who had been complaining about group projects since October.

"It's the opposite," the man said, already turning back to his screen. "It's the only reason anything here is worth anything."

Before Nathan could ask what he meant, Mr. Horváth herded them into a seminar room for the promised debate exercise, and Nathan found himself assigned to argue against Matilda, who had drawn the position that scientists were evenly split on climate change. Matilda, who did not believe a word of it, delivered her side with theatrical reluctance, folding her arms and saying, "That's what my uncle says. Half of them think it's us, half don't. It's a coin flip."

Nathan had prepared nothing, because he had assumed, wrongly, that knowing things was the same as being able to produce them. He stood there with his grandfather's voice in his head, his grandfather who called climate scientists grifters and had once, at Thanksgiving, accused Nathan of maligning an entire profession just for quoting a temperature at him. Nathan had hung up that night feeling both right and cruel, and he had not sorted out the two since.

"I don't actually know the numbers," Nathan said, which was not how debates were supposed to start. "But I know how the lab here works, sort of. The guy in there, he's redoing someone's count because a journal made him. Nobody takes one result and runs with it. So when my grandfather says it's fifty-fifty, he's imagining two teams of scientists yelling at each other, and I don't think that's the picture. It's more like everyone redoing everyone's homework until the answer stops moving."

"That's very poetic," said Matilda. "Do you have a number, or only a mood?"

The graduate student, who had drifted in to steal the leftover coffee, raised her hand as though she were the seventeen-year-old. "There's a paper," she said. "A 2013 study led by a guy named John Cook. They looked at 11,944 climate paper abstracts, and of the abstracts that took a position at all, 97.1 percent endorsed human-caused global warming." She set down the cup. "The part people miss is the 'took a position' part. Most abstracts don't say anything either way. That's why it's ninety-seven of the ones that do, not ninety-seven of everything."

Nathan wrote it on his hand, because his notebook was in the bag Bria was sitting on. On the bus home he held the number up against his grandfather again, and it did not do what he wanted it to, which was to settle the argument forever. His grandfather would ask who counted the papers, and who checked Cook, and whether checking was itself a position, and Nathan understood, sitting in the dark with the window rattling, that the answer to all of that was yes, they checked, that was the entire machinery, and that this would not convince a man who thought the machinery itself was the scam. He could hold both of those at once, though it felt like carrying water in his hands.

"Your grandfather is going to say the polity is rigged," Matilda said, watching him.

"He's going to say the scientists picked the abstracts."

"Did they publish how they picked?"

Nathan looked at his palm, where the ink had smeared into something between a statistic and a bruise, and said, "I'll find out before Thanksgiving."

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Spanish news writers often attribute a claim with 'según', meaning 'according to', which tells a reader the statement comes from a source, not the reporter.
story:
The apartment they'd rented in Granada had a narrow balcony where the morning sun arrived before anyone else did, and Nolan took his coffee there with the newspaper his father had bought from the kiosk, hoping the ink would rub off on him somehow. Three years of Spanish class, and here he was hiding from the waiter downstairs. He unfolded the paper and found a short article on page eleven, something about a dispute over water rights in a valley he'd never heard of. His teacher, Ms. Baptiste, had given the whole class an assignment before summer break: while abroad, read one article in the language of the country, and summarise it aloud, recorded, sent to her by the end of July. He'd put it off for two weeks, telling himself he needed the right article, a quiet morning, a mood of readiness that never quite materialized.

The first paragraph went slowly. He recognized maybe two words in five, and the gaps kept turning into guesses he didn't trust. Then his phone buzzed: Anaelle, from three hundred kilometers north, where her family was staying in a rented flat in Seville. She'd already sent her recording, she said, a whole minute of summary, and Ms. Baptiste had replied with a single word, "Bien." Nolan typed back that he was working on it, which was a generous description of sitting on a balcony holding a newspaper like a prop.

The article's second paragraph contained a sentence he read four times. It opened with a word he'd seen before but never in this position: "según." Según the farmers' association, the new canal would cut their allocation by nearly half. He checked the dictionary app, then closed it, uneasy. The dictionary said "according to," but the article's tone, as far as he could parse a tone in a language he half owned, treated the claim almost as settled. If he summarised it as fact, he'd be saying something the reporter had never said.

He thought of an argument from the spring, when he'd told his mother that video games ruined concentration, citing something he'd half heard in a hallway. She'd asked him where he'd read that, and he'd said he didn't remember, and she'd let it go in a way that still bothered him, because it meant she'd decided not to press, and he'd decided not to admit. There was a small ascetic pleasure, he noticed now, in refusing to pass along a claim you couldn't source, a kind of fasting from easy certainty. Though pleasure might be the wrong word. It felt more like a debt.

He texted Anaelle the sentence, just the sentence, no context. She replied ten minutes later with a voice memo, breathless from a staircase: "Según, sí. My article had it too. It means 'according to.'" He played it twice. In her article, she said, the phrase was "según the Ministry," and at first she'd taken the whole statement as the newspaper's own view, until she realized the word was doing something, marking the sentence as borrowed. "So who's saying it?" Nolan typed. "The source, not the reporter," she answered, and then a string of messages about a fountain she'd found near the cathedral, because Anaelle could hold a grammar point and a fountain in her head at once.

Nolan went back to the balcony. The farmers' association was claiming the cut; the regional government, según its own spokesperson, was claiming something milder, a redistribution, a technical adjustment. The reporter, as far as he could tell, had asserted nothing except that both sides had spoken. That was its own kind of honesty, or possibly its own kind of cowardice, and he couldn't decide which, sitting there with the sun moving across the tiles. He thought about texting his father to ask, but his father's instincts ran toward cynicism, toward the belief that all attribution was smoke, and that way of thinking had a causality problem, as Ms. Baptiste once put it about another topic entirely: it explained everything, so it explained nothing.

He set the phone on the rail, propped against the newspaper, and started recording. His summary came out in careful, ugly Spanish, full of pauses. The article concerned a dispute over water in the valley. Según the farmers' association, the canal would reduce their share. Según the government, the change was procedural. The newspaper reported both claims and offered no verdict. He said it that plainly, and his accent flattened the double r in "reducir," and a pigeon on the railing startled him mid-sentence so that he said "perdón" out loud to nobody, and he left that in.

Before sending it, he considered one more time whether to smooth the stumbles, to propitiate an invisible grader with a cleaner take. He'd done that on oral exams before, sacrificed accuracy for fluency, and it had worked, mostly, which was the part that stayed unresolved. He sent it unedited. Then he sat with the paper in his lap while his father filled a glass at the tap, and Anaelle's next message arrived, a photograph of the fountain with water catching the light in a way no summary could carry.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: Need-blind admission means a college decides whom to admit without considering whether the applicant can afford to pay; many US colleges are instead need-aware.
story:
The envelope had not arrived, but the spreadsheet had, and Stella had organized it into columns the way other people organized prayer. Twelve colleges down the left side, deadlines across the top, and a new column she had added on Tuesday night under the heading money?, which she filled with question marks because she did not yet know what belonged there. It was Thursday, fifth period, free study in Mr. Chatterjee's room, and she was counting question marks when Aditya leaned across the aisle.

"You're doing the thing," he said. "The hovering thing. Sit down inside your own chair."

"This is my chair. I'm just not all the way in it." She turned the laptop so he could see. "Here's the problem. Some of these schools decide who gets in without looking at whether you can pay. Some of them look. And nobody tells you which ones are which, at least not in the brochure."

Miah pulled her chair around from the next table, uninvited, the way she did everything. "Wait, that's legal? They can just check if you're poor before they let you in?"

"That's what I found out last night," Stella said. "The ones that don't look, they call it need-blind. The rest, most of them actually, are need-aware. Need-aware is the word. It means they look at your finances when they're deciding."

Mr. Chatterjee, watering the philodendron by the window that no one had asked him to water, made a small sound that was not quite a word. Stella ignored him, because if she let an adult explain anything right now she would lose the thread of her own thinking, and the thread was all she had.

"Okay," Miah said, "so drop the need-aware ones."

"It's not that simple." Stella scrolled, and the column of question marks scrolled with her. "The need-blind schools are harder. Way harder, statistically, I mean, not in a way I can prove, just in the way everyone knows. If I apply only where the money doesn't count against me, I'm applying to the places with the lowest odds. If I keep the need-aware ones, I might get in and then get an aid package that guts my family anyway, because getting in isn't the same as affording it. Either way I'm betting something." She stopped scrolling. "And the thing is, I can't even be angry about it cleanly, because if I ran a school with a small endowment, I'd probably be need-aware too. You can't abrogate arithmetic. You can't just decide the budget doesn't exist."

Aditya frowned at the word, and Miah said "abrogate?" and Stella waved her hand, meaning later, meaning it means what it means when you cancel something that was never really a rule.

She spent that weekend doing the unglamorous thing, which turned out to be the solution, though it did not feel like one at the time. She went through each college's financial aid page, one at a time, late at night with her mother asleep in the next room, and she sorted the twelve schools into three groups instead of two: need-blind, need-aware, and need-aware-but-historically-generous, which was a column she invented and labeled with a word she then deleted because it sounded like she was claiming a lineage of scholarship kids going back generations, and she wasn't, she was just the first one, which was its own kind of weight. By Sunday she had a list that looked like a strategy: four reaches where the money wouldn't count against her, four where it would, four safeties she could nearly afford outright. She emailed it to no one. She taped it inside her locker like a map of a country she had not yet been permitted to enter.

The answers came in March, two rejections, one deferment, and then, on a Tuesday with sleet on the windows, an acceptance from the second group, a need-aware school that had looked at her finances, weighed them, and taken her anyway, with an aid letter that left a gap her mother called "the eleven thousand dollar question." Stella sat with the letter at the kitchen table and understood that she had solved the wrong problem, or solved the right problem into a new one, and that this was probably what deciding things was made of.

She brought the letter to fifth period on Thursday to show Miah and Aditya, because a thing like that should be witnessed. Mr. Chatterjee was at the philodendron again. He read her face before he read the paper, and he said, quietly, not like a speech at all, "My wife works in admissions. She'd tell you the sagacious move is to call them and negotiate."

"There's nothing to negotiate. The number's the number."

"That's what they'd like you to believe," he said, and turned back to his plant. Stella looked at the letter, at the gap, at her own neat handwriting on the taped list visible in her mind's edge, the whole architecture of columns and question marks. Then she got out her phone and dialed the number, and while it rang she realized that the school had known everything about her money from the very beginning, and had still said yes. It was the need-blind schools, the ones that never asked, that had said no.

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: Ignoring air resistance, launch angles that add up to 90 degrees, such as 30 and 60 degrees, give the same range on level ground at the same speed.
story:
Anna crouched in the backyard with a plastic projectile launcher, a stopwatch, and a notebook whose last three pages were already substrate for a scrawl of arrows, half-finished equations, and one drawing of a sad-looking parabola. The physics test was on Monday, and Ms. Demir had said, on her way out of the lab, that the problems would all involve splitting a projectile's velocity into horizontal and vertical components, which Anna had nodded at and understood nothing of. Zane sprawled on the porch steps eating chips, and Daniela sat cross-legged in the grass, turning the stopwatch over and over like a coin she was deciding whether to spend.

"Set it to thirty degrees," Anna said. She wanted data. She wanted something to happen that she could measure, because the textbook's version of learning, where a worked example descended from above and was absorbed, had so far produced nothing but a headache.

Daniela set the angle, pulled the release, and the little yellow ball arced out over the lawn and dropped into the flowerbed by the fence. Anna wrote down the distance, counting fence boards like a surveyor. Then, because Zane insisted that a steep launch would obviously go farther, "more height, more glory," Daniela set the launcher to sixty degrees and fired again. The ball climbed high enough that Anna lost it against the sun, came down hard, bounced once, and rolled to a stop.

It stopped in the flowerbed. Not near the flowerbed, in it, a board and a half from the first ball, closer than either of them could have placed it by hand.

"That's broken," Zane said, around a chip. "One of those didn't count."

Anna fired both angles again, and then a third time, crouching each time to mark where the balls landed with stones from the garden edge. The thirty-degree shot and the sixty-degree shot kept arriving at the same place, give or take the width of her hand. She sat back on her heels. In her notebook she had been drawing the velocity as a single arrow, one line from the launcher to the sky, and somewhere in the ferment of that afternoon it occurred to her that the arrow was a lie of convenience. The ball was doing two things at once: it moved across the yard at some steady horizontal pace the whole flight, and it rose and fell at a pace that gravity kept rewriting. Thirty and sixty. They added up to ninety, and they landed in the same spot, and she did not yet know why, only that the two motions had to be taken apart before they could be put back together.

She tried it on paper. If the launch speed was the same both times, then the steep shot spent most of its speed going up, which meant less going across, and the shallow shot spent most of its speed going across, which meant less going up, and the trade apparently evened out. She couldn't prove it. She could only see it in the flowerbed, which for the moment felt like the same thing, and she was honest enough with herself to write in the margin, in small letters, that she did not fully get this yet.

"So which one wins?" Daniela asked, watching Anna's pencil move. "Thirty or sixty?"

"Neither. They tie." Anna tapped the two stones. "Thirty and sixty. Same range, same speed. It's like the angle doesn't care which half of the ninety you give it." She felt the shape of something she couldn't yet say: that two completely different-looking paths could be secretly equal, and that the way to see the equality was to refuse to look at the path as one thing.

Zane leaned over the launcher, suddenly less nonchalant, and turned the dial to forty-five. "Fine," he said. "Middle of everything. Best of both." He pulled the release before Anna could say that she hadn't tested that one, that she had no idea yet what forty-five meant, that her whole notebook was two data points and a suspicion.

The ball left the launcher at its flattest, fastest angle yet, cleared the fence entirely, and there was a soft thump from the next yard. They stood very still. Then Ms. Demir's head appeared over the fence line, the yellow ball held up between two fingers, her expression unreadable.

"You three," she said, "are going to learn trigonometry over my tomato plants."

activity: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
knowledge_domain: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
fact: In 1902, French colonial authorities in Hanoi paid a bounty for each rat tail, and people began cutting off tails and releasing the rats to breed, so the rat problem grew.
story:
The motion on the board behind Ms. Esposito read "This house would pay students for good grades," and Blake had been assigned to argue for it, which was unfortunate, because he no longer believed it.

He'd believed it on Monday, when he'd signed up with the smug confidence of a boy who had just read three studies. He'd stopped believing it on Tuesday, at dinner, when his sister proposed paying their younger brother a dollar per chore and his mother had put down her fork and told a story. In 1902, she said, French colonial authorities in Hanoi had paid a bounty for each rat tail, and people had begun cutting off the tails and releasing the rats to breed, so the rat problem had grown. Blake had laughed, then stopped laughing, then gone upstairs and sat with the story like a stone in his pocket for three days.

"I still don't get why you're freaking out," Emery said in the library an hour before the debate. She was flipping his cue cards into two piles, keep and burn. "You're supposed to argue the side. That's the whole game. It doesn't have to be your soul."

"It's not my soul. It's just that I found the crack and now I can't unsee it." He pulled a card back from the burn pile. "The bounty worked, technically. People brought in tails. The colonial authorities got exactly what they paid for."

"Because they got the metric wrong."

"Because the metric was the only thing they could see." He heard himself getting too loud and lowered his voice. "A tail isn't a dead rat. Everyone in this room knows what a grade is and isn't."

Klara dropped into the chair across from them with her laptop already open. She was arguing against the motion, which was the other problem. "I just want to say good luck and also I'm going to destroy you," she said. "Also, what's an incentive, philosophically? Because my second speaker keeps using it like it means money, and I think it means anything that bends a choice."

"That's the word I couldn't find," Blake said, and wrote it down.

The debate was held in Ms. Esposito's room after last period, desks shoved into a horseshoe, eleven people and a timer that beeped like a dying bird. Klara opened well. She talked about intrinsic motivation, about how the thing you pay for becomes the reason you do it, about altruistic impulses that curdle when you attach a price to them. "People who donate blood for money donate less blood over time," she said. "The payment crowds out the motive. You haven't bought more of the behavior. You've replaced it."

When his turn came, Blake stood, arranged his cards, and felt the whole room waiting for the version of him from Monday. "My side will tell you that paying for grades works," he said. "And they're right. It works the way the French bounty in Hanoi worked in 1902." He saw Klara's head come up sharply, because this was her material and he was stealing it, and he kept going anyway. "The authorities paid for each rat tail. People cut off the tails and released the rats to breed, so the rat problem grew. They paid for tails, and tails is what they got. Nobody paid for fewer rats, because nobody could count fewer rats." He set the cards down. "If we pay for grades, we will get grades. We will get grade-grubbing, renegotiated deadlines, the easiest AP we can find, a strategic relationship with learning. We will get tails."

"That's my case," Klara said from across the horseshoe, not into the microphone, just to him.

"I know."

"So what's yours?"

"I'm getting there." He was aware of Ms. Esposito watching him with her chin on her hand, not stopping him, and he understood that she had assigned the sides randomly and that randomness had handed him this. "Here's the problem with what I just said," he went on. "My opponents will tell you the story of a kid who works two jobs, whose parents never went to college, who would study harder for fifty dollars a month, and that story is true too. The crowding-out research comes mostly from people who had the luxury of being motivated in the first place. So we're weighing a real gain for a few against a real cost spread thin over everyone. That's a trade-off. Nobody in this room can resolve it with a slogan."

Klara's rebuttal was good, better than his speech honestly. She called his position an asymptote, an answer that gets closer to wisdom the longer you talk without ever touching it, and the room laughed, and Blake laughed too, because it landed.

Afterward Emery proselytized in the hallway about how he'd thrown the round and didn't care, didn't he see that he'd actually won the room, but Klara caught up with him at the lockers. "You know you lost, right? On the rubric. I got the team points."

"I know."

"So why do you look like that?"

He thought about his sister's dollar per chore, still on the fridge, unchallenged. "Because I argued my way out of believing something and into not knowing what to believe, and I'm not sure that's progress. Or maybe it is. Maybe that's just what a real answer looks like, and I hate it."

Klara considered him for a second, then held out her phone. "Emery's ordering pizza. You're coming."

He shut his locker and followed her down the hall, the beeping timer still going off in the empty room behind them.

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: The InVID-WeVerify browser plugin, built by a European Union-funded project, splits a video into key frames that can be reverse-searched.
story:
The video reached Thomas through Trent, who shoved his phone across the counter of Kelly's Phone Repair between customers. On the screen, a bridge buckled under brown water, a guardrail folding like wet cardboard, and the caption said it was the Millbrook crossing, gone under last night's storm. Thomas felt the small jolt that everyone in town must have felt at once, the vertigo of seeing a place you know swallowed. He had crossed that bridge two days ago. The clip was eleven seconds long and by noon it was everywhere, and Trent was already forwarding it.

"You're sharing that?" Maelie asked. She had come in to pick up a screen protector and stayed, leaning against the display case of refurbished cases.

"It's Millbrook," Trent said. "Everybody's posting it."

Thomas turned his own phone over in his hands without unlocking it. Last summer his mother had dragged him to her office for a take-your-kid day he'd found unbearable, all fluorescent light and stale biscuits, except for one hour when a colleague named nothing he remembered had seen him scrolling and rolled her chair over. She'd shown him a browser plugin on her work computer, something the office used for checking footage that came in from the field. She'd said it was built by a European Union-funded project, and she'd clicked a button and the video she was testing had fractured into still images, key frames, she called them, which she then dropped into a reverse image search one by one. He had been more enraptured by that than by anything else that day, though he hadn't known why until now.

"I want to check something," he said, and pulled his laptop out from under the counter where he kept the diagnostic tools.

Mr. Kelly looked up from a dismantled tablet. "On my time, it's on your break."

"On my break," Thomas agreed, and took the eleven seconds and loaded them into the plugin. It split the video into key frames, and he fed the clearest frame, the one with the buckling guardrail, into a reverse image search. Trent watched over his shoulder with the impatient energy of someone waiting for a page to load. Maelie watched too, but she was watching Thomas's face, which is why she saw it change before the screen did.

The results came back in a grid. The same bridge, the same brown water, the same folding guardrail, dated four years earlier and half a world away, in a provincial town whose name Thomas couldn't pronounce. There was no Millbrook anywhere in the results. There was no last night.

"That's the same shot," Trent said slowly, as if saying it faster might break it.

"It's the same frame. It's the same video." Thomas scrolled. Four years. A different river, a different country, and a caption that had travelled further than the truth could. He felt strange about it, a mixture of relief and something colder, because the clip had been beautiful in a way, and now that beauty belonged to somebody else's disaster. Somewhere that flood had been real, had ruined someone's harvest or someone's shop, and here it was wearing his town's name.

Trent pulled out his phone and went quiet, which for Trent was a kind of labour. "I already sent it to like six people," he said finally. "Including my mum. She's texting the neighbours about the bridge."

"So tell them," Maelie said.

"It looks like I'm an idiot."

"It looks like you found out," she said. "There's a difference, but only if you say it out loud."

Thomas thought about how quickly the thing had moved, faster than any correction could move, and how fake footage like this had become endemic online, so common it was practically native to the environment, like mold in a student flat. He didn't say that out loud. What he said was, "Send them the frame I searched. Send them the dates. People can look at two pictures and decide for themselves." He turned the laptop so Trent could screenshot it.

Trent typed for a while, deleted, typed again, and sent something to his mother. Then he looked up. "What's that thing called, the plugin?"

"InVID-WeVerify," Thomas said. "It splits a video into key frames that can be reverse-searched." He said it the way the colleague had said it, plain, like the name of a tool and not a verdict.

Mr. Kelly drifted over, drying his hands on a cloth, and studied the grid of four-year-old results. "Half the town's sharing that thing," he said. "You want to put that on the shop's page? We've got the screens for it."

Thomas looked at the search results, then at the door, where the afternoon light was catching the dust from Mr. Kelly's repair bench. He pulled the laptop back toward himself and started copying the link.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: A Sikh gurdwara's langar serves free vegetarian meals to anyone regardless of religion, caste or status, and people traditionally eat together seated on the floor as equals.
story:
Aiden had told Ocean to wear something with a covered head, and now, standing at the shoe shelves inside the gurdwara entrance, he watched his friend pull a bandana from his jacket pocket and shake it out like a magician producing a dove. "It's all I had," Ocean said. "It has a skate shop logo on it." Aiden looked at the small printed wheels, then at the rows of heads ahead of them, scarves and handkerchiefs in every colour, and decided it would do. His mother was already three steps ahead, carrying the box of prashad she had promised the aunties she would bring, and his grandmother followed behind her with the unhurried certainty of someone who knew exactly where the sweets table would be.

The hall smelled of cardamom and hot oil and the faint mineral damp of concrete floors washed that morning. It was the day of the Vaisakhi celebration, and the corridor thrummed with it, children running with paper flags, an uncle arguing cheerfully about parking, a man with a kettle of tea moving through the crowd like a boat through choppy water. Aiden felt the strange double pull he always felt here, half belonger and half guide, because Ocean had asked him last week, in the flat tone he used when trying not to seem curious, whether he could come along and see it. "My dad thinks all religions are machination," Ocean had said, spinning a pencil across his notebook. "Like schemes, basically." Aiden hadn't argued. He had just said come and see.

Inside the main hall they sat cross-legged behind his mother while the kirtan filled the room, harmonium and tabla and a voice that rose and folded back on itself. Ocean sat very still, which for Ocean was a kind of speech. When the ardas ended and the granthi walked past with kirpan glinting at his waist, Ocean leaned over and whispered, "Is he allowed to carry that in here?" and Aiden said, "He's the one most allowed." Ocean nodded slowly, as though filing the answer somewhere he could examine later.

Downstairs, the langar hall was already filling. Long mats ran the length of the floor, and volunteers moved along the rows with steel buckets of dal and trays of roti, serving anyone who sat, everyone facing the same direction, everyone at the same height. Ocean paused at the doorway with his tray. "So we just sit anywhere?" Aiden pointed at a stretch of mat between two families he didn't know and an elderly man he did. "Anywhere on the floor," he said. "Langar. It's free, it's vegetarian, and it doesn't matter who you are, what religion or caste or anything. Everyone eats together sitting down. Equals." Ocean looked at him, then at the hall, a banker in a suit cross-legged beside a student in a hoodie, and said, quietly, "Your dad should see this."

They sat, and the servers came. A woman Aiden had never met spooned dal onto both their trays without asking who they were, and the old man beside them, Mr. Ong from the corner shop, leaned over and told Ocean that in forty years of coming here he had never once been asked to pay, and that once a businessman sat where Ocean was sitting and ate with his hands because he'd forgotten his fork and nobody said a word. "Nobody's above anybody down here," Mr. Ong said, tapping the mat. "That's the whole point of the floor." Ocean ate his roti thoughtfully, tearing it in neat pieces.

Aiden's grandmother settled across from them with her own tray and began her quiet campaign, which was to feed Ocean until he surrendered. "Beta, more dal," she said, signalling to a server before Ocean could answer. Aiden knew her want without needing it spoken: she wanted the friend fed, wanted the table full, wanted proof, in the shape of second helpings, that the world still worked the way she trusted it to. What Aiden himself wanted was harder to say out loud. He wanted Ocean to understand this place without Aiden having to translate it into something smaller, and at the same time he wanted to know whether it would survive the translating, whether a thing built on equality could be shown off without becoming a performance.

After the meal they carried their plates to the washing station, where teenagers in damp sleeves took them two at a time. Ocean rolled up his sleeves and joined the line of scrubbers without being asked, and Aiden felt something in his chest exhilarate, quick and light, watching his friend's hands work through the grey water. It wasn't proof of anything, Aiden knew that. One afternoon of washing dishes didn't settle any argument about religion or scheme or sincerity, and later, walking out through the corridor past the shoe shelves, Ocean would probably say something sharp and half-joking, because that was how Ocean kept his balance. Aiden didn't have a considered position yet on whether any of it was true in the way his grandmother meant true. He only knew that the floor had held everyone, and that he had wanted to be on it.

The bandana came off at the entrance, and Ocean folded it carefully, wheels inward, and put it back in his pocket. Outside, the afternoon was ordinary, traffic and pigeons and a man selling corn from a cart as if the cart were autochthonous to that corner, as if it had grown there. Ocean turned the folded cloth over once in his hands. "Same time next month?" he said.
